screens:
The session begins.

The Trade Way ends here, in a jam of wheels, hooves and tempers beneath the grey arch of the Basilisk Gate. The sun is low over the Sword Coast and the first lanterns are flickering along the wall. Somewhere beyond the stone is Baldur's Gate — the city from the stories, where a goddess told you that you would learn how to serve her. She did not say how.

At the table under the arch a Flaming Fist sergeant with a scarred chin and an ink-stained ledger waves the next traveller forward, asks a question, and writes without looking up. A halfling in a patched green coat slips along the queue, calling out: "Clean beds, Outer City prices, no fleas worth mentioning!"

Behind you, a slap of cards on wood and a burst of laughter: the caravan guards have started another hand on an upturned barrel. A gust of wind lifts a card off their makeshift table, and it skids to a stop against your boot, face-down. The cat looks at it, then at you.

The man in front of you is waved through. The sergeant dips her quill and looks up. "Next. Name, and what brings you to the Gate?"

Sergeant Varn's eyes go to your hands first, then to the coin on its cord. She looks at it for about as long as she'd look at a cart's axle. The quill scratches: *Worgen, J.*

"Upper City gates shut at full dark." She doesn't check the sky. She doesn't need to. "That's under the hour. Walk fast, don't take the river lanes, and you'll reach the inner wall in time. The Watch is another matter. Armed stranger after the lamps are lit, nobody inside to speak for him? They'll turn you round, Lady's Hall or not." She blots the line. "The Hall opens at dawn. The Lady keeps the same hours as everyone else."

She jerks her chin at the arch. "Through. Keep the blade in its sheath inside the walls. Next."

You've taken two steps when a heavy tread catches up behind you. It's the big sunburned guard from the barrel game, the one who's been laughing loudest all the way down the queue. He drops to a crouch where you left the card, scoops it up without turning it over and tucks it into his deck with a quick, almost relieved flick.

"Thanks for not treading on it, friend. Rurik Dunmore." He straightens up with a grin. His eyes go to the cat on your shoulder before they come back to you. "We're short a fourth since Hobb lost his shirt at Beregost. Copper stakes, nothing that'd hurt a man. You play?"

Behind him the other guards are already squaring the deck on the barrelhead. A few paces off, the halfling in the green coat has stopped calling about beds. She's pretending to fix a button and listening to every word.

The cat's tail has gone very still.

Rurik's grin slips for a moment. It's the look of a man who's just had a sure thing turn him down.

"Copper's copper, friend. Nobody ever lost a farm at copper." He tips his head at the barrel, where the other two are squaring the deck and watching. "One hand. I'll stake you myself, then it's not even your coin..." He hears himself, stops, and scratches at the peeling sunburn on his neck. "No. Fair enough. A promise is a promise. My old man made a few. Shame he never kept one."

He starts to turn away, then turns back with his thumb on the edge of the deck. He slides one card out and holds it up face-down between two thick fingers. The back is lacquered and catches the lantern-light. In its centre is a small silver seal: a circle split straight down the middle.

"Look, this one's yours more than mine. Blew right to you, didn't it." He laughs, but it comes out short. "Turned up in my deck at a table in Beregost. Never had it before. I've lost every hand it's been in since. You're going to the Lady's Hall anyway. Take it, leave it on her altar, and let her sort it out."

The cat's claws come through your cloak and prick your shoulder. It's holding on hard.

Before you can answer, a patched green coat squeezes between you and Rurik's elbow.

"Elfsong, he'll say, he always says the Elfsong. That's the Lower City, eight silver a night, and the singing ghost keeps you up till dawn." Tamsin Reedfellow beams up at you. Her button looks perfectly fine now. "Tamsin Reedfellow. Three silver, a clean bed, a lock on the door, and it's two streets from the gate. Your boots stay where you put them, and I'll swear that on anything you like. And the Hall opens at dawn, so you'd be first up the hill tomorrow instead of last through the gate tonight." She glances at the cat, then at the card, and then very carefully looks at neither. "The kitty's free."

Rurik is still holding the card out, face-down.

Rurik snorts. "Faith? Habit. You don't pull a card mid-run, that's how a man admits he's beaten." He turns the card over in his fingers without looking at it. "And I did pull it. Left it on the table at the Jovial Juggler, in Beregost. That's the inn by the smithies, with the painted fool on the sign. Next morning it was back in my deck. I figured one of the lads put it back as a joke." He glances at the two by the barrel. Neither of them laughs. "Nobody owned up."

He shrugs, a big rolling shrug, and flips the card face-up.

It isn't paper. It's a thin slip of ivory gone the colour of old butter, lacquered so heavily the paint seems to sit under glass. You've handled a hundred decks, Talis, Three Dragon, cheap Calishite pasteboard, and this one comes from none of them. There's no suit and no number. A gold coin stands on its edge in the middle of the card, balanced the way no coin really balances. On its left a woman leans toward it with a smile, her hair loose and her hand open. On its right, where a second figure ought to be, there's only a pair of black antlers rising out of darkness, painted so carefully that every tine has its own small highlight.

You know those antlers. Anyone who prays to the Lady learns to know them early. They're Beshaba's, the Maid of Misfortune's, the sister nobody toasts.

The painter gave neither side the coin. It stands between them, waiting to fall.

The cat makes a sound you've never heard from it, a low, thin note in its chest. It's not quite a growl. It doesn't take its eyes off the card.

Down by your elbow, Tamsin Reedfellow has stopped pretending not to look. She stares at the face for one long breath, and then her gaze slides away to the lanterns on the wall.

"Sun's going," she says, lighter than before but not quite as fast. "Whatever you two decide about pictures, the bed's still three silver."

Rurik holds the card up between you, face out now. "There. Now you've seen it." He wets his lips. "So. Altar or no?"

You don't press her. You just wait, with the cat's weight on your shoulder and the noise of the queue all around, and that does more than pressing would have. Tamsin's patter runs out.

"Not the picture." It comes out low and slow, nothing like her hawker's voice. "I've never seen that picture, and I'll be glad never to see it again, she's not a lady my people say out loud. It's the back." Her eyes flick to Rurik's fingers and away. "The little silver mark. The circle with the line down it."

She wets her lips.

"The lightermen fish dead men out of the harbour some mornings. Everybody in the Outer City knows that much. What they don't say so loud is that some of them come up with a coin between their teeth. Not the Fist's coin, not anybody's coin. It's old and flat and won't buy you a cup of anything. One of the boatmen brought one to my kitchen last winter, wanting to know if it was worth something. Circle split down the middle, just like that. Nobody would take it off him." She shrugs, but the shrug is stiff. "He threw it back in the river the next week. Said it made his oars slip."

Behind you, a quill stops scratching.

You don't have to turn far. Sergeant Varn is still at her table under the arch, with the next traveller standing in front of her waiting. Her pen is lifted over the ledger and her eyes are on Tamsin. She doesn't say anything. After a breath she dips the quill and writes again, slower than before.

Tamsin has seen it too. Her smile comes back with a snap, and her voice goes back up to street pitch.

"So that's no reason, is it, not a real one, just a boatman's story and a girl who doesn't like antlers. Take it to the Lady, maybe she'll know what to do with it, that's her business and not mine." She hitches her coat straight. "Three silver. Lock on the door. I'll walk you there myself before the lamps are all lit."

Rurik hasn't moved. He's scratching at the peeling sunburn on his neck with his free hand, and the card is still held face-out between the two of you.

"Coins in dead men's mouths," he mutters. "Lovely. You still want me holding it, friend, or are you taking it?"

Rurik doesn't wait to be asked twice. He lays the card face-down on the cloth as if it might bite, and as it leaves his fingers his shoulders drop. His whole big frame seems to let out a breath.

"Lady's luck to you, friend. Better yours than mine." He wipes his hand on his trousers without seeming to notice. "No promises. That's fair. That's more than fair." He's already backing toward the barrel. "Hobb's seat's still open if you ever break that promise of yours. Copper stakes." He grins, and it's nearly his old grin.

You fold the cloth over once, then twice. Through the layers the ivory feels warmer than it should after an evening in a caravan guard's fist. It's more like a stone that has sat in the sun all day. You put it in the pouch, away from your own deck. The cat watches it go in, then watches the pouch. Its claws come out of your shoulder one at a time, but its tail stays still.

Tamsin's face falls a little when she hears you aren't coming for the bed, and then it brightens again. She wasn't counting on you.

"Your name stays with me, and mine stays with you, that's a fair trade." She points through the arch. "Straight through, up the hill, always up. Don't turn toward the water, whatever the Sergeant says about river lanes she's right, they wind about and smell like eels. Follow the cart ruts with the fresh straw in them. That's where the patriars' carriages go, and they always know the way home. Ruts end at the gate. If the Watch turns you round, my door's on Tallow Row and the latch is down till midnight." She hesitates, and for once she doesn't fill the gap. "Mind where you sleep with that thing in your pouch, that's all."

She's off along the queue before you can thank her again. "Clean beds, Outer City prices!" Her voice comes back a little too loud.

You've taken one step toward the arch when wood taps on wood behind you. Twice.

Sergeant Varn hasn't got up. The traveller in front of her has been waved through, and the one behind him is still fumbling at his pack. She uses the gap and doesn't look at the queue.

"Worgen." It isn't loud. "A word. Two minutes, and you'll still make the inner gate." Her quill points at the empty space at the end of her table, out of the lantern's main glare. "The thing in your pouch. Where did the caravan man say he got it?"

Varn doesn't open the ledger. She reaches inside her tabard and takes out a second book, a small one bound in oilcloth with its corners worn round, and writes in it with the same quill. *Jovial Juggler. Beregost. Returns to deck.* Her hand is smaller here than in the gate ledger, and tighter. She doesn't add your name.

When you ask your question she taps the quill twice on the oilcloth.

"Officially, no." Her voice stays flat. "Men in the harbour are drink and bad footing. That's how they're filed. The coin in the mouth is a sailor's joke. Somebody paying Umberlee."

She glances toward the queue. A carter with a cage of geese has reached her table and is waiting. She holds up one ink-stained finger at him without looking at him, and he waits.

"Unofficially." She closes the little book on the quill to keep her place. "I've held one of those coins. Flat, old, worn smooth at the edge. The mark on it was a circle cut straight down the middle. I didn't take a rubbing, and I've been sorry since." Her eyes come back to you and stay there. "Before I say anything more I'd want to see the two side by side. I'm not going to do that on a stranger's word, and I'm not going to do it from a halfling's kitchen story."

The cat has shifted its weight on your shoulder. It's watching her now and not the pouch, which hasn't happened all evening.

"Show me the back. Only the back. Keep it in your cloth, I don't want to touch it." The lantern catches the scar on her chin as she tilts her head toward the dim end of the table. "Then you can go up your hill. You've about half an hour."

James draws the bundle out of his pouch and turns back one fold of cloth, then a second, so that only the back of the card shows. The lacquer catches the lantern. Under the glaze the silver seal looks wet, as if it had just been pressed.

Varn doesn't lean in. She takes the lantern off its hook and holds it lower, at the height of the card. She looks at the seal the way she looks at a cart's wheel, all of it, unhurried, and then she looks again.

"The line." Her voice hasn't changed. "Doesn't run true through the middle. It's off to the left, a hair. The circle's thicker at the bottom, like the die was worn." She sets the lantern back on its hook. "Mine was the same. Same flaw. Struck from the same die, or one cut to copy it."

The cat leans forward on James's shoulder until its whiskers nearly touch the cloth. It sniffs once and pulls back.

Varn picks up the quill. She doesn't tap it this time. She writes one line in the oilcloth book and turns it so he can't read it.

"Cover it."

She waits until he has. Then she answers his question.

"I don't know the priests. I go to the Fist's chapel, and that's Tempus." She closes the little book on the quill. "And I'll tell you what I'd tell a recruit. The Hall is in the Upper City. It eats from the same tables as everyone else up there. I don't say anyone there is crooked. I say I don't know, and neither do you." Her eyes go to his pouch and come back. "Go at dawn. Show the back first, the way you showed me. Watch the face of whoever looks at it before you show them anything else."

The carter with the geese clears his throat. Varn holds up the finger again without looking at him.

"The coin isn't on me. I can lay hands on it, and I have notes. Dates. Where the boats found them." She says it flatly, like a list of supplies. "Tomorrow at noon. The Fist boathouse under the Seatower causeway, in the harbour. Ask for me at the door by name. Not by the card." A beat. "If you're coming, say so now. I've got geese."

Varn nods once. She doesn't write it down, which tells you she won't forget it.

"Noon." Then she turns to the carter. "Name. Business." The geese start honking behind you as you go.

The arch swallows the noise of the queue, and then the city takes over.

Beyond the wall the street climbs at once, cobbles worn into shallow bowls, houses leaning in close overhead with their upper floors almost touching. The air smells of tar, fried fish and wet stone. Lamplighters are already working the crossings with long poles, and every lamp they light seems to darken the sky a little. You find the ruts where Tamsin said they'd be: two grooves in the cobbles with fresh straw caught in them, gold under the lamps. You follow them up.

It's steep, and you walk it fast. The cat rides with its weight pressed against your neck and doesn't look at the shops or the people. Twice it turns its head and looks back down the hill, then faces forward again. You see nothing behind you but the evening crowd going home.

The houses get taller and cleaner as you climb, and the streets get quieter. Then the ruts end at a wall of pale dressed stone. In it is a gate with its leaves half drawn, and two lanterns burn above it. Four men of the Watch stand there in blue and silver, with halberds, and their boots are polished. One of them is already looking at your rapier.

"Evening." The one with a corporal's knot on his shoulder steps half into your way. He's polite. "Gate shuts in a quarter hour. Business in the Upper City?"

Before you can answer, someone comes up the last stretch of the hill behind you, a little out of breath. It's a young woman in the Lady's blue, with a silver coin hanging at her throat. She carries a lantern in one hand and a wicker basket in the other, half full of folded slips of paper, a few copper coins and a bunch of wilting marigolds.

"Corporal Dask. Last round." She lifts the basket for him to see. Then she sees you, and then the cat, and she stops on the cobbles.

For a moment she just stares at it. It's a careful kind of staring, like someone trying to remember where she's seen a face.

The corporal sighs. "Novice Pell collects petitions at the lower markets every dusk. The Hall reads them at dawn." He looks back at you. "So. You've no one inside to vouch for you, I'm guessing, and you're carrying steel. That's not coming through tonight, friend. If it's the Lady you want, give the girl your slip."

Pell has come back to herself. She sets the lantern on the stone ledge by the gate and takes a scrap of paper and a stub of charcoal from the basket.

"I can carry a name and a few words up." She's speaking to you, but her eyes keep going to the cat. "What should I write?"

Pell doesn't answer right away. She looks at the cat properly now, not in quick glances, and the cat looks back at her from your shoulder. It blinks once, slowly, the way cats do when they've decided someone isn't a threat. Then it turns its head and goes back to watching the dark street behind you.

"No." It comes out too quickly. She hears that herself and starts again. "I mean, I've never seen him before. Not a real cat. Not this one." Her hand goes to the silver coin at her throat and stays there. "I can't say more than that. It isn't mine to say, it's... I'm sorry. I only carry the basket."

Behind her, Corporal Dask shifts his weight and looks up at the lanterns over the gate. He doesn't say anything yet.

Pell steadies the scrap of paper on the stone ledge and holds the charcoal over it. She writes slowly, sounding the words under her breath: *James Worgen. Come at the Lady's bidding, seeking how to serve her.* Then she stops, with the charcoal still touching the paper.

"The elders read every word on these. Every one, even the ones about lost goats." She swallows. "May I put that you came with a cat? Just that. Nothing else, if you'd rather not."

The cat's tail stirs once against your collar and goes still.

· Time passes: 3 minutes

Place: Inner Gate of the Upper City · Time: Day 1 · evening

Pell's charcoal moves again, slowly. *Came with a cat.* She looks at the words for a moment, as if she isn't sure she's allowed to have written them, and then folds the slip once.

When you ask about tonight she doesn't answer straight away. She looks at the basket and then up the dark street past the gate, where the roofs climb toward the temples.

"The slips go on the reading table. Everyone's. That's how it's done." She turns the folded paper over in her fingers. "But there's one who sits up late. Mother Tessaly. She doesn't sleep much any more." She stops herself before she says anything else. "I can ask her. I can't say she'll come down, or send anything. I can only ask."

Corporal Dask sighs through his nose and looks up at the lanterns.

"Gate shuts at full dark. Leaves closed, bar down. If anyone sends word for you after that it comes through the wicket, and I'll be the one opening it." He tips his halberd toward a stone bench set into the wall, a few yards from the arch and out of the lantern glare. "You can wait there, friend. Not under the arch, and not with your hand near that blade. If nobody's come by the second bell, nobody's coming."

Pell tucks your slip into her sleeve and leaves it out of the basket. She picks up her lantern and goes through the gate at something close to a run. You can hear her shoes on the cobbles for a long way.

A quarter of an hour later the leaves swing shut with a deep wooden boom. The bar drops into its brackets. Three of the Watch go inside the wall, and Dask stays at the wicket in the lantern light with his back to the door. He's watching the street the way a man watches weather.

You sit on the cold bench. The city goes on below you without you: a dog somewhere, a shutter banging, a cart's iron tyres a long way down. Full dark comes the way it does near the sea, all at once. The cat climbs down from your shoulder into your lap, turns round twice and doesn't settle. It faces downhill, toward the bend where the straw-rut road disappears between the tall houses and the last lamp burns at the corner.

It's been doing that since the Basilisk Gate.

James nudges the basin aside with his boot and lifts the shutter bar. He keeps his shoulder to the wall and opens the shutters first, then the casement. He has to raise the iron hook out of its eye, the same hook the blade was working at a minute ago. The frame sticks where it has warped, then gives. Cold air comes in off the harbour, wet and smelling of tar and fish.

The cat answers the order with a short *yes* and jumps onto the end of the sill, by the hinge side. He sits tucked into the corner of the frame with his ears turned outward and his nose working.

James takes a copper from his purse, closes his fingers on it and says the word. The coin lights up in his palm with a clean, steady white glow, like a candle without the flicker. He holds it out past the sill at arm's length.

The lean-to roof spreads out below him, wet slate shining under the light. The sneak's path is easy to follow. Near the sill, two slates have been knocked out of line where the man crouched. Below that a long, smeared scrape runs straight down the slope, and three or four slates have come loose and slid. At the bottom edge, about six feet down and a little to the left of the window, the lead gutter shows a dark smear along its lip. It's blood, from a hand grabbing at it on the way over.

The thing he dropped is lying in the gutter. It's a dagger, narrow and plain, with a blade no wider than two fingers. It must be what slid between the casement and the frame. The grip is wrapped in dark cord. It lies crosswise in the lead channel, half in a puddle of rainwater, and the point catches the light.

James leans out a little further and takes in the rest.

The roofline above the window is empty: ridge tiles, a chimney stack, a gable end next door, with nothing on them or behind them. The alley under the lean-to is narrow, cobbled and wet. Right below the edge of the roof there are broken slate fragments on the stones and a dark scuffed patch where the man came down. From there a line of wet marks goes off toward the single lamp at the far end, irregular, one print clear and the next one dragged. Past the lamp the alley turns a corner, and nothing moves there. There's a rain barrel against the kitchen wall, a stack of empty crates, and a closed kitchen door with light leaking under it from a banked oven.

The cat breathes in the night air for a long moment. What comes down the bond is the smell of the alley: wet stone, kitchen ash, the sour trace of the man's blood going cold. There's nobody fresh out there and nobody close.

The light from the coin shines out across the wet roof. Anyone at the far end of the alley, or on a roof across the way, can see a lit window. James can't see anyone looking back.

The dagger lies in the gutter, six feet below the sill and out of reach of his arm.

*2) The watch order to the cat: he answered "yes" and took up his post on the hinge end of the sill.*

*4) Looking for what he dropped: the dagger was out in the open in the gutter, under your light, and nobody was hiding on the roof or in the alley, so your passive Perception 11 was enough.*

I leave the card face-down and step up to the table, keeping my hands clear of my weapons.

“James Worgen. Looking for work, and paying my respects at the Lady’s Hall.” I lift the worn coin on its cord briefly. “Can I still reach it before the Upper City gates close, Sergeant?”

“Used to.” My eyes linger on the deck before I meet Rurik’s gaze. “Trouble was, I never stayed at copper stakes. Promised I’d stop.”

I offer him a rueful smile. “Good luck with your fourth. Before you go—know a decent inn on the way toward the Lady’s Hall? Somewhere a man can sleep without having to guard his boots.”

I steady the cat with a hand, but leave the card in Rurik’s fingers.

“An unfamiliar card turns up in your deck, and you keep playing with it? You’ve more faith than I have.”

I study the split-circle seal without touching it. “Where in Beregost? And show me the face, would you? I’m not agreeing to carry it yet.”

“Not an ordinary losing card, Rurik. That’s Beshaba beside the Lady. Keep hold of it a moment.”

I turn to Tamsin, my voice quiet rather than accusing.

“Three silver sounds fair. But you’ve gone rather anxious to get us away from this conversation. Have you seen that picture before—or something like it? If you know a reason I shouldn’t carry it to the Hall, I’d be grateful to hear it now.”

I glance at her ledger, then back to her. “Does that split circle mean something to you, Sergeant? I’d rather know before I carry it through half the city.”

I draw out the wrapped card and carefully uncover only its back, holding it in the cloth where Varn can see the seal.

“If it matches, is there someone at the Lady’s Hall you trust with this?”

“Noon, the boathouse. I’ll be there. Thank you, Sergeant.”

I tuck the covered card away and leave her to the geese, heading uphill toward the inner gate. Half an hour is still time to ask whether the Hall will receive me.

“James Worgen. I’ve come at the Lady’s bidding, seeking how to serve her.”

I leave my hands well away from the rapier and turn slightly toward Pell, giving her a clear look at my companion.

“But before you write that down—do you recognise the cat?”

“Put the cat down too. He’s done his share of the walking.”

I give her a small smile. “I won’t press you for someone else’s confidence. But if someone at the Hall is expecting him, could you get that note to them tonight? I can wait here while you ask.”

“Dawn, garden door. Thank you, Pell—for taking the trouble, and for telling me.”

I tuck the sealed note inside my cloak and stroke the cat’s back. Through our familiar bond, I ask him silently: *You’ve been watching behind us since the gate. Is someone following us? Show me what you’re worried about.*

I rise from the bench, leaving my blade sheathed.

“Corporal, someone’s followed me from the Basilisk Gate and waited down at that bend the whole time I’ve been here. I’m not looking for a fight. I’d appreciate a witness.”

Keeping near the gate’s lantern light, I call downhill: “If you’re waiting for me, you’ve waited long enough. Come into the light and tell me what you want.”

“James, not squire. And I haven’t hired you yet.”

I keep my tone easy and stay beside the gate. “Two silver for a safe walk is reasonable. Following me for an hour before offering it makes me wonder what else I’d be agreeing to. Who are these folk—and what have you told them I’m carrying?”

“Two silver to the Elfsong. Just a guide’s fee—no protection arrangement, no debt, no promises beyond tonight. Agreed?”

I count out two silver, ready to pay if he accepts, and nod to Dask. “Thank you, Corporal.”

To the cat, silently: *Stay close. Let me know if anyone else takes an interest in us.*

“A room, please.” I put the eight silver on the bar. “James Worgen. I need to be at the inner gate at first light—could someone knock early enough for me to walk up?”

I enjoyed playing James here. The strongest parts were the atmosphere, the NPCs, and the way small choices led naturally into trouble. I ended the session wanting to meet Mother Tessaly and find out what the card meant.

**What worked**
- The NPCs had distinct voices and interests. Varn’s guarded professionalism, Tamsin’s salesmanship, and Jory’s polite evasions made conversations worth having.
- James’s background mattered immediately. The offered card game tested his promise without forcing him to break it, and the cat was a useful companion with personality.
- I could solve problems by talking and taking precautions. Calling the follower into the Watch’s light and warning the burglar both worked without becoming compulsory fights.
- Concrete details supported decisions: closing gates, the dawn appointment, the window latch, and the accessible roof. That makes me hopeful about the eventual heist.

**What broke**
- The roll system repeatedly used **+2 instead of +7** for Persuasion and Intimidation. Narration corrected the results, but the displayed record remained wrong. Worse, my correction couldn’t reach the GM until I pressed Onward. There needs to be a way to flag a bad roll while its card is pending.
- The burglary scene was narrated in full, then paused for a check about something that had already happened, then repeated almost verbatim after the roll. Resolve checks at the point of uncertainty, before narrating their consequences.
- Interface updates leaked information James hadn’t learned: “Guild Sneak on the Roof” and the Guild faction tag effectively identified the intruder’s affiliation while the story said I hadn’t discovered who sent him.
- The opening character record contradicted the supplied sheet and campaign rules in places, notably rapier proficiency, the Healing Light limit, and attunement. Those discrepancies need settling before play.

**What was missing or could improve**
- **More progress per turn.** An entire session covered arrival, several conversations, supper, and part of a night. Those scenes were good individually, but the larger premise barely came into view. I wanted to reach at least the first substantial briefing about Tymora’s task.
- Routine transactions could be compressed. The gold-to-silver-to-copper exchanges received more attention than they needed.
- Out-of-game explanations were often longer than necessary, especially explanations of why ordinary actions required no roll. A short correction is useful; a numbered audit of opening a window interrupts the mood.
- The details of precautions need to stay physically consistent. I intended the basin to fall noisily if the shutters opened; the narration placed it on the floor while still treating it as that alarm.
- The mystery offered several warnings and withheld answers in succession. A firm, actionable discovery sooner would give me more to plan around.

Overall: a compelling city and good character interaction, held back by unreliable roll integration, occasional information leaks, and slow pacing. Keep the grounded NPCs and respect for player choices; tighten the routine scenes and let the central adventure arrive sooner.

Yes—the clearest was retrieving and examining the burglar’s dagger. I’d lit the roof and checked the alley specifically to work out a safe way to recover it. Then the session ended. I wanted to turn that intrusion into something I could investigate, rather than just another warning that someone was interested in me.

I also wanted to challenge the incorrect Persuasion modifier **before accepting the roll’s outcome**. I tried, but the interface wouldn’t send my message while the card was pending. Pressing Onward felt like accepting a result I knew was wrong, even though the GM subsequently corrected it.

By contrast, not chasing the burglar was deliberate: James had an important dawn appointment and wasn’t going to scramble onto wet slates just because somebody ran. That felt like a character choice, not a restriction.

He drops to a crouch where you left the card, scoops it up without turning it over and tucks it into his deck with a quick, almost relieved flick.

Behind him the other guards are already squaring the deck on the barrelhead. A few paces off, the halfling in the green coat has stopped calling about beds. She's pretending to fix a button and listening to every word.

Rurik snorts. "Faith? Habit. You don't pull a card mid-run, that's how a man admits he's beaten." He turns the card over in his fingers without looking at it. "And I did pull it. Left it on the table at the Jovial Juggler, in Beregost. That's the inn by the smithies, with the painted fool on the sign. Next morning it was back in my deck. I figured one of the lads put it back as a joke." He glances at the two by the barrel. Neither of them laughs. "Nobody owned up."

It isn't paper. It's a thin slip of ivory gone the colour of old butter, lacquered so heavily the paint seems to sit under glass. You've handled a hundred decks, Talis, Three Dragon, cheap Calishite pasteboard, and this one comes from none of them. There's no suit and no number. A gold coin stands on its edge in the middle of the card, balanced the way no coin really balances. On its left a woman leans toward it with a smile, her hair loose and her hand open. On its right, where a second figure ought to be, there's only a pair of black antlers rising out of darkness, painted so carefully that every tine has its own small highlight.

You know those antlers. Anyone who prays to the Lady learns to know them early. They're Beshaba's, the Maid of Misfortune's, the sister nobody toasts.

The painter gave neither side the coin. It stands between them, waiting to fall.

The cat makes a sound you've never heard from it, a low, thin note in its chest. It's not quite a growl. It doesn't take its eyes off the card.

Down by your elbow, Tamsin Reedfellow has stopped pretending not to look. She stares at the face for one long breath, and then her gaze slides away to the lanterns on the wall.

"Sun's going," she says, lighter than before but not quite as fast. "Whatever you two decide about pictures, the bed's still three silver."

Rurik holds the card up between you, face out now. "There. Now you've seen it." He wets his lips. "So. Altar or no?"

Rurik doesn't wait to be asked twice. He lays the card face-down on the cloth as if it might bite, and as it leaves his fingers his shoulders drop. His whole big frame seems to let out a breath.

"Lady's luck to you, friend. Better yours than mine." He wipes his hand on his trousers without seeming to notice. "No promises. That's fair. That's more than fair." He's already backing toward the barrel. "Hobb's seat's still open if you ever break that promise of yours. Copper stakes." He grins, and it's nearly his old grin.

You fold the cloth over once, then twice. Through the layers the ivory feels warmer than it should after an evening in a caravan guard's fist. It's more like a stone that has sat in the sun all day. You put it in the pouch, away from your own deck. The cat watches it go in, then watches the pouch. Its claws come out of your shoulder one at a time, but its tail stays still.

Tamsin's face falls a little when she hears you aren't coming for the bed, and then it brightens again. She wasn't counting on you.

"Your name stays with me, and mine stays with you, that's a fair trade." She points through the arch. "Straight through, up the hill, always up. Don't turn toward the water, whatever the Sergeant says about river lanes she's right, they wind about and smell like eels. Follow the cart ruts with the fresh straw in them. That's where the patriars' carriages go, and they always know the way home. Ruts end at the gate. If the Watch turns you round, my door's on Tallow Row and the latch is down till midnight." She hesitates, and for once she doesn't fill the gap. "Mind where you sleep with that thing in your pouch, that's all."

She's off along the queue before you can thank her again. "Clean beds, Outer City prices!" Her voice comes back a little too loud.

You've taken one step toward the arch when wood taps on wood behind you. Twice.

Sergeant Varn hasn't got up. The traveller in front of her has been waved through, and the one behind him is still fumbling at his pack. She uses the gap and doesn't look at the queue.

"Worgen." It isn't loud. "A word. Two minutes, and you'll still make the inner gate." Her quill points at the empty space at the end of her table, out of the lantern's main glare. "The thing in your pouch. Where did the caravan man say he got it?"

turns.message:
I step to the end of her table and keep my voice low.

“The Jovial Juggler, in Beregost. He says it appeared in his deck there. Tried leaving it on the table; next morning it was back among his cards. Could have been someone’s joke. I didn’t see it happen.”

I glance at her ledger, then back to her. “Does that split circle mean something to you, Sergeant? I’d rather know before I carry it through half the city.”
turns.reply:
Varn doesn't open the ledger. She reaches inside her tabard and takes out a second book, a small one bound in oilcloth with its corners worn round, and writes in it with the same quill. *Jovial Juggler. Beregost. Returns to deck.* Her hand is smaller here than in the gate ledger, and tighter. She doesn't add your name.

When you ask your question she taps the quill twice on the oilcloth.

"Officially, no." Her voice stays flat. "Men in the harbour are drink and bad footing. That's how they're filed. The coin in the mouth is a sailor's joke. Somebody paying Umberlee."

She glances toward the queue. A carter with a cage of geese has reached her table and is waiting. She holds up one ink-stained finger at him without looking at him, and he waits.

"Unofficially." She closes the little book on the quill to keep her place. "I've held one of those coins. Flat, old, worn smooth at the edge. The mark on it was a circle cut straight down the middle. I didn't take a rubbing, and I've been sorry since." Her eyes come back to you and stay there. "Before I say anything more I'd want to see the two side by side. I'm not going to do that on a stranger's word, and I'm not going to do it from a halfling's kitchen story."

The cat has shifted its weight on your shoulder. It's watching her now and not the pouch, which hasn't happened all evening.

"Show me the back. Only the back. Keep it in your cloth, I don't want to touch it." The lantern catches the scar on her chin as she tilts her head toward the dim end of the table. "Then you can go up your hill. You've about half an hour."

turns.message:
I draw out the wrapped card and carefully uncover only its back, holding it in the cloth where Varn can see the seal.

“If it matches, is there someone at the Lady’s Hall you trust with this?”
turns.reply:
James draws the bundle out of his pouch and turns back one fold of cloth, then a second, so that only the back of the card shows. The lacquer catches the lantern. Under the glaze the silver seal looks wet, as if it had just been pressed.

Varn doesn't lean in. She takes the lantern off its hook and holds it lower, at the height of the card. She looks at the seal the way she looks at a cart's wheel, all of it, unhurried, and then she looks again.

"The line." Her voice hasn't changed. "Doesn't run true through the middle. It's off to the left, a hair. The circle's thicker at the bottom, like the die was worn." She sets the lantern back on its hook. "Mine was the same. Same flaw. Struck from the same die, or one cut to copy it."

The cat leans forward on James's shoulder until its whiskers nearly touch the cloth. It sniffs once and pulls back.

Varn picks up the quill. She doesn't tap it this time. She writes one line in the oilcloth book and turns it so he can't read it.

"Cover it."

She waits until he has. Then she answers his question.

"I don't know the priests. I go to the Fist's chapel, and that's Tempus." She closes the little book on the quill. "And I'll tell you what I'd tell a recruit. The Hall is in the Upper City. It eats from the same tables as everyone else up there. I don't say anyone there is crooked. I say I don't know, and neither do you." Her eyes go to his pouch and come back. "Go at dawn. Show the back first, the way you showed me. Watch the face of whoever looks at it before you show them anything else."

The carter with the geese clears his throat. Varn holds up the finger again without looking at him.

"The coin isn't on me. I can lay hands on it, and I have notes. Dates. Where the boats found them." She says it flatly, like a list of supplies. "Tomorrow at noon. The Fist boathouse under the Seatower causeway, in the harbour. Ask for me at the door by name. Not by the card." A beat. "If you're coming, say so now. I've got geese."

turns.message:
“Noon, the boathouse. I’ll be there. Thank you, Sergeant.”

I tuck the covered card away and leave her to the geese, heading uphill toward the inner gate. Half an hour is still time to ask whether the Hall will receive me.
turns.reply:
Varn nods once. She doesn't write it down, which tells you she won't forget it.

"Noon." Then she turns to the carter. "Name. Business." The geese start honking behind you as you go.

The arch swallows the noise of the queue, and then the city takes over.

Beyond the wall the street climbs at once, cobbles worn into shallow bowls, houses leaning in close overhead with their upper floors almost touching. The air smells of tar, fried fish and wet stone. Lamplighters are already working the crossings with long poles, and every lamp they light seems to darken the sky a little. You find the ruts where Tamsin said they'd be: two grooves in the cobbles with fresh straw caught in them, gold under the lamps. You follow them up.

It's steep, and you walk it fast. The cat rides with its weight pressed against your neck and doesn't look at the shops or the people. Twice it turns its head and looks back down the hill, then faces forward again. You see nothing behind you but the evening crowd going home.

The houses get taller and cleaner as you climb, and the streets get quieter. Then the ruts end at a wall of pale dressed stone. In it is a gate with its leaves half drawn, and two lanterns burn above it. Four men of the Watch stand there in blue and silver, with halberds, and their boots are polished. One of them is already looking at your rapier.

"Evening." The one with a corporal's knot on his shoulder steps half into your way. He's polite. "Gate shuts in a quarter hour. Business in the Upper City?"

Before you can answer, someone comes up the last stretch of the hill behind you, a little out of breath. It's a young woman in the Lady's blue, with a silver coin hanging at her throat. She carries a lantern in one hand and a wicker basket in the other, half full of folded slips of paper, a few copper coins and a bunch of wilting marigolds.

"Corporal Dask. Last round." She lifts the basket for him to see. Then she sees you, and then the cat, and she stops on the cobbles.

For a moment she just stares at it. It's a careful kind of staring, like someone trying to remember where she's seen a face.

The corporal sighs. "Novice Pell collects petitions at the lower markets every dusk. The Hall reads them at dawn." He looks back at you. "So. You've no one inside to vouch for you, I'm guessing, and you're carrying steel. That's not coming through tonight, friend. If it's the Lady you want, give the girl your slip."

Pell has come back to herself. She sets the lantern on the stone ledge by the gate and takes a scrap of paper and a stub of charcoal from the basket.

"I can carry a name and a few words up." She's speaking to you, but her eyes keep going to the cat. "What should I write?"

turns.message:
“James Worgen. I’ve come at the Lady’s bidding, seeking how to serve her.”

I leave my hands well away from the rapier and turn slightly toward Pell, giving her a clear look at my companion.

“But before you write that down—do you recognise the cat?”
turns.reply:
Pell doesn't answer right away. She looks at the cat properly now, not in quick glances, and the cat looks back at her from your shoulder. It blinks once, slowly, the way cats do when they've decided someone isn't a threat. Then it turns its head and goes back to watching the dark street behind you.

"No." It comes out too quickly. She hears that herself and starts again. "I mean, I've never seen him before. Not a real cat. Not this one." Her hand goes to the silver coin at her throat and stays there. "I can't say more than that. It isn't mine to say, it's... I'm sorry. I only carry the basket."

Behind her, Corporal Dask shifts his weight and looks up at the lanterns over the gate. He doesn't say anything yet.

Pell steadies the scrap of paper on the stone ledge and holds the charcoal over it. She writes slowly, sounding the words under her breath: *James Worgen. Come at the Lady's bidding, seeking how to serve her.* Then she stops, with the charcoal still touching the paper.

"The elders read every word on these. Every one, even the ones about lost goats." She swallows. "May I put that you came with a cat? Just that. Nothing else, if you'd rather not."

The cat's tail stirs once against your collar and goes still.

place.name: Inner Gate of the Upper City

stats.depthReason: no tension signal; the base of the range (deep only for «важный ход» or a combat climax)

turns.message:
“Put the cat down too. He’s done his share of the walking.”

I give her a small smile. “I won’t press you for someone else’s confidence. But if someone at the Hall is expecting him, could you get that note to them tonight? I can wait here while you ask.”
turns.reply:
Pell's charcoal moves again, slowly. *Came with a cat.* She looks at the words for a moment, as if she isn't sure she's allowed to have written them, and then folds the slip once.

When you ask about tonight she doesn't answer straight away. She looks at the basket and then up the dark street past the gate, where the roofs climb toward the temples.

"The slips go on the reading table. Everyone's. That's how it's done." She turns the folded paper over in her fingers. "But there's one who sits up late. Mother Tessaly. She doesn't sleep much any more." She stops herself before she says anything else. "I can ask her. I can't say she'll come down, or send anything. I can only ask."

Corporal Dask sighs through his nose and looks up at the lanterns.

"Gate shuts at full dark. Leaves closed, bar down. If anyone sends word for you after that it comes through the wicket, and I'll be the one opening it." He tips his halberd toward a stone bench set into the wall, a few yards from the arch and out of the lantern glare. "You can wait there, friend. Not under the arch, and not with your hand near that blade. If nobody's come by the second bell, nobody's coming."

Pell tucks your slip into her sleeve and leaves it out of the basket. She picks up her lantern and goes through the gate at something close to a run. You can hear her shoes on the cobbles for a long way.

A quarter of an hour later the leaves swing shut with a deep wooden boom. The bar drops into its brackets. Three of the Watch go inside the wall, and Dask stays at the wicket in the lantern light with his back to the door. He's watching the street the way a man watches weather.

You sit on the cold bench. The city goes on below you without you: a dog somewhere, a shutter banging, a cart's iron tyres a long way down. Full dark comes the way it does near the sea, all at once. The cat climbs down from your shoulder into your lap, turns round twice and doesn't settle. It faces downhill, toward the bend where the straw-rut road disappears between the tall houses and the last lamp burns at the corner.

It's been doing that since the Basilisk Gate.

You follow its gaze and see only the lamp, a doorway, and a rain-barrel at the corner. A woman goes by with a covered basket and doesn't look up. Nothing else moves. The cat goes on staring at the bend anyway, ears forward, and its tail twitches once at the tip.

Somewhere above you a bell strikes once.

Not long before the second bell, the wicket rattles. Dask says something low through the grille, listens, and opens it a hand's width. Pell squeezes out sideways with her lantern. Her cheeks are red from the hill and her hair has come loose from its pins.

"She was awake." She has to stop and breathe. "She read it. Twice. Then she held it to the candle to read it again, as if the words might change." She takes a folded square of paper out of her sleeve, sealed with a blob of blue wax. A thumb was pressed into the wax while it was warm, and an old coin set into it, so the Lady's face is printed under the whorls of a thumbprint. "She says come at dawn. Not to the front steps. The garden door, on the lane behind the Hall, before the reading. Show this to whoever opens it. And bring him." She looks down at the cat in your lap.

She doesn't hand the paper over yet.

"She asked me what colour his eyes are." Pell says it carefully, as if she's carrying something full to the brim. "I didn't know. I told her I'd look."

She crouches and holds the lantern a little lower. The cat turns its head away from the bend in the road at last and looks up at her, straight into the light.

Pell looks for a long breath. She doesn't say what she sees. She stands up and puts the sealed paper in your hand.

"One more thing." Her voice drops so that Dask, three yards off, won't hear. "Brother Corvan was at the reading table when I came in. He doesn't usually sit up. He saw me take your slip out of my sleeve instead of the basket, and he asked me what I had." She swallows. "I said a petition. He said all petitions go on the table. Then he watched me go up the stairs." She touches the coin at her throat and lets go of it. "I don't know that it means anything. I just thought you should know who'd seen."

Behind her, Dask clears his throat and puts his hand on the wicket.

turns.message:
“Dawn, garden door. Thank you, Pell—for taking the trouble, and for telling me.”

I tuck the sealed note inside my cloak and stroke the cat’s back. Through our familiar bond, I ask him silently: *You’ve been watching behind us since the gate. Is someone following us? Show me what you’re worried about.*
turns.reply:
Pell ducks her head at the thanks. The colour in her cheeks is from more than the hill.

"It was only a slip of paper," she says. She doesn't sound as if she believes it. Dask's hand is still on the wicket, and she backs toward it. "Dawn. The lane behind, past the well with the green pump. The door's the one with no handle on the outside." She slips through sideways with her lantern. The wicket shuts after her, and the bolt goes home.

Dask settles his back against the door again and goes back to watching the street.

You tuck the note inside your cloak, against your ribs, and run your hand down the cat's spine. Under your palm he's stiff as wire. You reach for him the way the pact lets you, mind to mind, and ask.

The answer doesn't come in words. It never does. It comes as a lean of attention, his attention pressed onto yours, and the bend in the road comes forward. The lamp. The doorway. The rain-barrel. With it comes the world as he gets it, mostly through his nose. Wet stone, horse, tallow smoke from the lamp. Under all of that is something warm and sour that doesn't belong to stone.

The cat can't fix it to a place. The scent comes off the bend in pieces. One breath it's near the barrel, the next it's somewhere in the dark of the doorway. Then the sea wind comes up the hill and smears it across the whole corner, and he loses it. You feel his frustration through the bond, a sharp flick like a tail-tip.

What he's sure of comes through clearly enough. It's one person, not two. He smelled them in the queue at the Basilisk Gate, the same smell of lamp-oil and wet wool and something peppery, like a cheap pipe. He smelled them again twice on the climb, both times he looked back. Whoever it is stopped when you stopped, and they haven't left.

He gives you one more thing before he lets go. It isn't an image. It's the way he feels about the card in your pouch, a low, steady wariness, and this is not that. It's the plain dislike a cat has for a stranger in his yard.

Then the bond goes quiet again, and he goes back to staring at the bend with his ears forward.

Down the hill, the corner lamp gutters in the wind and steadies. Nothing moves there. Behind you, Dask shifts his halberd from one hand to the other and says nothing. As far as he's concerned your business with the Watch is over.

It's a little before the second bell. The Upper City is shut until dawn. Tamsin's latch on Tallow Row stays down until midnight, and the Elfsong is down in the Lower City. Whoever is at the bend is between you and both of them.

turns.message:
I rise from the bench, leaving my blade sheathed.

“Corporal, someone’s followed me from the Basilisk Gate and waited down at that bend the whole time I’ve been here. I’m not looking for a fight. I’d appreciate a witness.”

Keeping near the gate’s lantern light, I call downhill: “If you’re waiting for me, you’ve waited long enough. Come into the light and tell me what you want.”
turns.reply:
James gets up off the bench. His hands stay well away from the hilt.

Behind him Corporal Dask lets out a slow breath through his nose. He doesn't move away from the wicket.

"I keep this gate. I don't leave it." He shifts the halberd into the crook of his arm. "But what happens in my light, I see. And I'll remember it."

James steps to the edge of the lantern glow and calls down the hill. His voice carries in the quiet. The cat jumps from the bench to his boot and stays there, ears forward.

For a moment nothing happens. The corner lamp sways. Somewhere below, a shutter bangs again.

Then a figure separates from the doorway beside the rain-barrel. It doesn't hurry and it doesn't hide. It's a lean man in a wet wool coat buttoned to the throat, with a long lamplighter's pole on his shoulder, brass hook at the top, and a dented oil can swinging from his belt. He has a clay pipe in his teeth. When he comes up into the light the smell arrives with him: lamp-oil, damp wool, and cheap peppery leaf. The cat's tail lashes once against James's ankle.

The man stops a good thirty feet off, just inside the edge of the lantern light, and lifts two fingers to his cap.

"Evening, squire. Corporal." He takes the pipe out and points the stem down the hill. "Round's done. I was having a smoke out of the wind, that's all. Didn't mean to give anybody a turn."

"Lamps on this stretch were lit at sunset," Dask says flatly. "I watched them lit. Wasn't you."

The man looks at the corporal, then at James, then down at the cat, and his easy face doesn't change at all. He taps the pipe bowl against his teeth twice, like someone deciding which pocket to pay out of.

"No," he says pleasantly. "Wasn't me." He drops the pretence like an empty sack. "Name's Jory. No harm meant, squire, and none done. There's folk down the hill who like to know who's new in town and what he's carrying. They like it best when he gets where he's going in one piece, too. Newcomers with heavy purses turn up in the river otherwise, and that's bad for everybody's business." He settles the pole on his other shoulder. "The Upper City's shut till dawn, and you've the look of a man with nowhere booked. Two silver and I'll walk you to any door you like, Outer City or Lower. Nobody so much as brushes your sleeve on the way."

He puts the pipe back between his teeth and smiles round it.

"So where'll it be tonight?"

stats.depthReason: DM hint: tense; the base of the range (deep only for «важный ход» or a combat climax)

turns.message:
“James, not squire. And I haven’t hired you yet.”

I keep my tone easy and stay beside the gate. “Two silver for a safe walk is reasonable. Following me for an hour before offering it makes me wonder what else I’d be agreeing to. Who are these folk—and what have you told them I’m carrying?”
turns.reply:
Jory takes the correction with a little dip of the pipe stem, like a shopkeeper who's been told the price is wrong and doesn't much mind.

"James, then." He looks at you, then at the corporal behind you, and his smile stays where it is. You let the silence after your question run on. You aren't in a hurry, and you make sure he can see that.

It doesn't work on him. Jory has been on the wrong end of a patient silence before, and he waits it out while his pipe draws.

"Fair question. Wrong man to ask it of." He takes the pipe out of his mouth. "Following's the job. The offer's just me being friendly. And who they are?" He tilts the stem down the hill toward the roofs and the dark harbour past them. "Folk who like the nights quiet and the river empty. You'll hear the stories soon enough. Everybody does."

He settles the pole on his shoulder.

"As for what you're carrying, I haven't told anybody anything. Not yet. Nothing to tell but a man and a cat sitting on a cold bench." He gives you a cheerful look that says he knows exactly how much he isn't saying. "Whatever's in your pouch is your business, James. Until somebody decides it's theirs. Then it helps to have friends who've heard of you."

Behind you Corporal Dask hasn't moved from the wicket. He shifts his weight once, the way a man does when he's listening and wants you to know it.

At your boot, the cat's tail lashes once.

"Two silver still stands," Jory says. "Or don't hire me, and I'll go home, and you can find your own way down in the dark. Either's fine by me."

*(Out of game: Persuasion 4 + 7 = 11 against 15. That's a failure. Jory gives you the polite street answer and nothing more.)*

turns.message:
“Two silver to the Elfsong. Just a guide’s fee—no protection arrangement, no debt, no promises beyond tonight. Agreed?”

I count out two silver, ready to pay if he accepts, and nod to Dask. “Thank you, Corporal.”

To the cat, silently: *Stay close. Let me know if anyone else takes an interest in us.*
turns.reply:
Jory listens to the terms the way a carter listens to a toll-keeper reading out the rates, nodding along at each one.

"A walk's a walk, James. No arrangement, no debt, nothing past the Elfsong's door." He points the pipe stem at you. "You've done business before, I can tell."

You open your purse and find only gold. The last hand you won paid out in gold, and nobody gave you change on the road. Jory sees the coin before you hold it out. He fishes in his coat, counts eight silver into your palm by feel without looking down, and the gold piece disappears somewhere under the wet wool.

*(Out of game: your purse held only gold, so the two silver went as one gold piece and Jory gave you eight silver back. If you'd rather have handled it another way, say so.)*

Behind you, Corporal Dask doesn't step away from the wicket.

"Leaves open at first light." He looks at Jory for a long moment, then at you. "I've seen his face. That's all I'm saying, friend."

You set off downhill. The cat takes its place on your shoulder again, and when you reach for it through the bond its answer is short: a flick of attention, *yes*, and then its nose goes to work.

Jory doesn't walk ahead of you, and he doesn't walk behind. He keeps a step off your left shoulder, so that anyone coming the other way sees two men out together, and the lamplighter's pole bobs over both of you. The straw-ruts carry you back down between the tall houses. Then he turns off them at a corner you'd never have picked. The street narrows and starts to smell of the river.

"Lower City starts about here. You can't see the wall for the houses built against it, so nobody bothers to look for it." He nods at a dark arch on the right. "Don't take that one. Short cut to the docks, and that's what everybody thinks for about half of it."

Halfway down a stepped lane a street lamp has guttered to a blue bead. Jory stops under it with a little sigh of professional duty, lifts the pole and reaches for the shutter with the brass hook. The hook misses, finds it on the second try, and opens it. The flame promptly goes out altogether. He looks up at the dark lamp for a moment.

"Not my round," he says, and walks on.

All the way down the cat keeps at it, nose up into the wind off the harbour. What comes back through the bond is plain: Jory's pepper and lamp-oil at your elbow, fish, tar, a tannery somewhere, a hundred strangers who passed and went their way. None of them comes back, and none of them stops when you stop. As far as the cat's nose can tell, the man you hired is the only one interested in you tonight. It doesn't relax, but its tail goes back to swinging.

Twenty minutes or so after the gate, the lane opens onto a wider street with lit windows. The noise of a full common room spills out onto the cobbles, along with the smell of ale and roast pork. The sign over the door shows a woman's face in profile with her mouth open, painted in faded blue.

Jory stops a few steps short of the light and doesn't go in.

"The Elfsong. Delivered whole, as agreed." He touches the pipe stem to his cap. "That's tonight done. If you ever want the other kind of arrangement, ask any lamplighter on the hill for Jory. Most of them'll even know who you mean." He's already turning away into the dark of the lane, pole on his shoulder. "Sleep well, James. If she lets you."

Inside it's warm, close and loud. Low beams are black with smoke, sailors and caravan hands sit at long tables, and a fire is going in the hearth. A dice game is rattling at the back, and you're glad it's dice. Behind the bar a broad woman with grey hair cropped short and forearms like a stevedore's is wiping down a tankard. She looks you over, then the cat, and her expression doesn't change.

"Mags. I keep the bar nights." She sets the tankard down. "Room's eight silver, with a bolt on the door and breakfast at dawn. The singing's free, and there's no refund for it." She tips her head at the ceiling. Somewhere up there, faint and far off, a woman's voice is starting a slow song in a language you know from your Elvish lessons and can't quite follow. Half the room doesn't even look up. "Room, or just a drink?"

I glance toward the sound overhead. “And what’s supper cost? Something hot before I turn in.”
turns.reply:
Mags doesn't count the silver. She sweeps it off the bar with the side of her hand, and it's gone into her apron before the last coin stops ringing.

"Worgen." She reaches under the bar without looking and puts down an iron key on a loop of tarred string. "Up the stairs, end of the passage, the door with the crack in it. The crack's old. The bolt's new."

When you ask about first light she snorts.

"Inner gate. You and the milk carts." She picks up the next tankard and starts wiping it. "Kitchen boy's up at the fourth bell to light the ovens. He'll bang on your door on his way down. If you're not up by then, you weren't going anyway. It's a good half hour up the hill at a fast walk, less if you know the stairs off Wyrm Lane. You don't."

Overhead the song climbs a little and holds a long note, so faint it might be coming through the beams or through the stone. Nobody at the long tables looks up. One sailor hums a bar of it into his ale, off-key, and his mate elbows him.

"She's in the walls," Mags says, before you can ask. "Goes on till the small hours, some nights longer. You get used to her or you don't."

The cat on your shoulder turns one ear toward the ceiling and then turns it back again. Whatever the singing is, it doesn't interest him. His nose has gone back to the room: the dice game at the back, the door, the stair.

"Supper's pork. That's all that's left." Mags jerks her chin at the kitchen hatch, where a pot is steaming. "Bowl, bread and a mug of ale, four silver. Water instead of ale, three." She sets the tankard down hard. "You've just given me your last silver. I'll break a gold piece, but you'll carry the change in copper. Bowl or not?"

New place: James's Room at the Elfsong
Promise: Early Knock at the Elfsong

turns.message:
“Bowl, bread and water. Copper spends.”

I hand Mags a gold piece, then take my supper to an empty seat away from the dice game, with a view of the door. Before eating, I rest a hand beside the cat and quietly say, “You’ve earned a better supper than hardtack. Let’s see how the pork is.”
turns.reply:
Mags takes the gold piece, bites it without any fuss, and drops it into her apron. Then she counts out the change from a clay jar under the bar in stacks of ten, one hand flat on top of each stack so the coins don't slide. That's seven stacks. They make a heavy little heap that goes into your purse with a sound like a handful of gravel.

"Three silver, seven back. In copper, like I said." She shoves a wooden bowl through the kitchen hatch, then a heel of bread and a cup of water that tastes faintly of the barrel. "Bowl comes back to the bar when you're done."

The table you pick stands against the side wall, half in the fire's shadow. From there you can see the street door, the foot of the stair and most of the room. The dice game at the back is behind your left shoulder, where you'd have to turn to watch it. The pork is better than the price: shoulder stewed down with onions until it falls apart, under a skin of fat, with pepper in it that somebody wasn't stingy with.

The cat comes down off your shoulder onto the bench beside your hand. When you speak to him he looks at the bowl, then up at you, as if deciding whether to be insulted. You tear off a strip of the meat and set it on the board. He sniffs it for a long moment, then eats it in three neat bites without hurrying. He washes one paw afterwards and puts his head back over the edge of the bowl. Through the bond you get a warm, satisfied feeling, and under it something you'd almost call *more*.

The second strip goes the same way. After the third he sits back and folds his tail round his feet, and his attention leaves the food for the room.

Behind you the dice rattle and stop. A man yells "Lady's own!" and slaps the table, and a groan goes up around him. The cat's ear turns toward the noise and turns away again. It's ordinary luck, men's luck, and none of his business. Overhead the song in the walls has slowed, the same few phrases going round like water in a millrace.

The street door opens twice while you eat. First come a pair of rope-burned deckhands who go straight to the bar. Then a girl comes in with a basket of eggs for the morning, and Mags pays her in copper without looking. The cat watches each of them from the doorway to wherever they stop, and then lets them go. Nobody looks at your table for longer than people look at a stranger with a cat.

By the time you mop the bowl with the last of the bread, the fire has burned down to a red bed. Half the long tables have emptied, and the dice game is down to three players. The stair to your room goes up into the dark at the end of the bar, and the key on its tarred string is heavy in your pocket.

+70 cps (Change from the gold piece for supper: 7 sp given as 70 copper, counted out in stacks of ten)

turns.message: I return the bowl to Mags and head upstairs with the cat. Before settling in, I check the room—the door’s crack and bolt, the window and its latch, and any space large enough to hide a person. If it’s clear, I close up and bolt the door.
turns.reply:
Mags takes the bowl without a word. She glances inside, sees it's been mopped clean with the bread, and drops it into the wash tub behind the bar. "Fourth bell," she says, and goes back to her tankards.

The stair is narrow and steep, and every tread creaks except the one you skip without thinking about it. The cat rides up on your shoulder. At the top the passage runs the length of the building under a sloping ceiling. Its few doors are shut, and a single candle in a tin sconce burns halfway along. You find yours at the far end. The crack is easy to spot: it runs down one panel from the top rail almost to the latch. It's an old split in the grain, filled at some point with pitch that has since shrunk. Lamplight from the passage shows through it in a thin line. Put your eye to it and you could see most of the room.

The key turns stiffly. Inside it's small and plain and smells of lye and old smoke. There's a bed with a straw tick and two blankets, and a washstand with a chipped jug. A low chest sits at the foot of the bed with its lid up and nothing in it. Pegs for clothes run along one wall, and in the corner a curtain hangs on a rod over a shallow alcove. You check the alcove first. It holds a chamber pot and a broom and nothing else. You crouch to look under the bed. There's barely a hand's width of space and a lot of dust, and nobody could fit there. The chest is too small for anyone but a child.

The cat jumps down while you look. He makes his own round, nose low along the skirting, along the bed frame and under the curtain. Nothing he finds bothers him. Through the bond you get stale tobacco from some earlier lodger, mice in the wall, and the faint sour smell of whoever scrubbed the floor. None of it is the pepper and lamp-oil.

The window is a single casement under the eaves. It has small panes of cloudy glass in lead and a pair of wooden shutters inside. When you open the shutters you can see that the casement's latch is a plain iron hook dropped into an eye. The frame has warped enough to leave a gap along the edge where the two meet, wide enough to slide a thin knife-blade through. Through the glass you see a lean-to roof of wet slate about six feet below the sill, probably the kitchen. It slopes down to an alley where a single lamp burns at the far end. A man could climb onto that roof from the alley with a barrel and some nerve, or come down onto it from the roofline.

The bolt on the door, though, is as good as Mags said. It's a heavy iron slide on a new plate, screwed into the frame. The wood around the screws is still pale where it was freshly cut. You shoot it home, and it seats with a solid clunk you feel through your hand.

Somewhere in the wall behind the bed, the singing goes on. It's slow and soft, the same few phrases round and round. The cat jumps onto the blankets, turns once and sits facing the window.

 *(Out of game: none of these needed a roll. Returning the bowl, checking an empty room nobody was hiding in and bolting the door had no real uncertainty and no cost for failing, so I narrated all three as done. One correction: you said "close up", and my text left the shutters open after you looked out at the roof. You also closed and fastened the inner shutters over the casement before you bolted the door. The casement's iron hook is still on the outer window behind them.)*

turns.message:
I hang my bedroll over the door’s split to block the view and set the empty washbasin beneath the window, where opening the shutters would knock it down.

Then I settle onto the bed, keeping the wrapped card separate from my deck and the rod within reach.

*Wake me if someone tries to come in,* I ask the cat through the bond. I touch Tymora’s coin. “Here I am, Lady. A little guidance tomorrow would be welcome.”

I turn in until the early knock.
turns.reply:
James drapes the bedroll over the top rail of the door. The thick wool falls across the split and swallows the thin line of passage light. He sets the empty basin on the floorboards under the shutters, close enough that the first shutter to swing in would hit its rim. The wrapped card goes on the near side of the bed and the deck on the far side, with the whole straw tick between them. The rod lies along the frame where his hand can find it in the dark.

The cat watches all this from the blankets. When the request comes down the bond he doesn't look round. What comes back is short and plain: *yes*. His gaze stays on the window.

The coin is cool under James's thumb. He says the words to the ceiling and the soot-black beams, and the singing in the wall goes on as if nobody spoke. He lies down. Sleep comes slowly, then all at once, the way it does after a long road.

He dreams of a table. It isn't a card table. There are no cards and no players, only green baize under one lamp. A gold coin stands on its edge in the middle of the cloth and spins. It spins for a long time without slowing or wobbling, and it doesn't fall. Every time the lamplight catches one face it's gone before he can see which face it was. Someone across the table is waiting for it to fall. He can't see who, only that they're patient.

Down in the real world the Elfsong empties and goes quiet. The common room shuts below him. A late door bangs. Somewhere past midnight the singing in the wall thins and stops.

A little before the half-hour, a man comes over the lean-to roof.

The cat hears him first. One slate shifts under a careful boot and clicks against the slate below it. It's a small sound, but nothing else in the building is making any.

James wakes all at once, without the grogginess. The jolt down the bond feels like claws in his mind, and the green table is gone. It's dark. The bedroll still hangs over the door, and the passage beyond it is silent. On the blankets by his knee the cat has gone flat, with his ears pinned forward at the shutters. What comes through the bond is sharp and close: *one. outside. on the roof.* A moment later a breath of wet air leaks in around the warped frame, and the cat adds a smell. It's wet leather and tar, and under them something sour and nervous. It isn't pepper, and it isn't lamp-oil. It isn't Jory.

Something scrapes on the other side of the shutters. It's thin and metallic, a blade sliding into the gap between the casement and its frame and feeling for the hook. It stops. Whoever it is heard nothing from inside and is listening. Then the blade starts again, slowly.

The shutters are still fastened, and the basin still sits under them. The man outside hasn't got the hook up yet.

changes.summary: New person: Guild Sneak on the Roof

stats.depthReason: DM hint: tense; the base of the range (deep only for «важный ход» or a combat climax)

turns.message:
I take up the rod and move quietly to one side of the window, out of the direct line through it.

“That’s far enough. Withdraw the blade and keep your hands where I can see them. Who sent you?”

I ready Eldritch Blast if the intruder attacks or forces the shutters—not if he backs away.
turns.reply:
James slides the rod off the bed frame. In the Boots of Elvenkind his feet make no sound on the boards. He crosses to the wall beside the window, out of line with the gap, and puts his back to the plaster with the rod's cool length against his palm. The cat stays flat on the blankets, watching him.

The blade outside lifts the hook a hair, and James speaks.

He doesn't need to raise his voice. The room is silent and the man's ear is a few inches from the wood.

On the other side of the shutters the scraping stops dead. For a long moment there's nothing at all, not even breathing. Then the blade slides back out of the gap, slowly and carefully, the way a man takes his hand out of a dog's kennel.

"Easy." It's a young voice, hoarse and too close to the shutters. "Easy, friend. Blade's out. See? Out." A slate clicks as he shifts his weight back. "Nobody's after you. Only meant to have a look, that's all, just a look, nobody said nothing about..."

He stops himself there. The next sound is a boot on wet slate, then another, quicker, as he backs down the slope of the lean-to away from the window.

He's backing off, so James's readied blast stays unspent in his hand.

The man gets three steps. Then he turns to run.

The slate is wet and he's moving too fast. His heel goes out from under him with a slick scrape and he comes down hard on his back. He slides the rest of the way down the lean-to in a rattle of loose slates and goes over the edge. Six feet below there's a heavy, wet thump in the alley, and a gasp that turns into a curse.

Something small and metal skitters down the slates after him. It stops with a click in the lead gutter at the roof's edge and stays there.

From the alley comes scrabbling, a hiss of pain, then uneven footsteps, one hard and one dragging. They go away from the building toward the single lamp at the far end. They don't stop at the lamp. They turn the corner and fade into the general drip and murmur of the Lower City at night.

Through the bond the cat gives James one long breath of the smell going away: wet leather, tar, and now fresh blood from a scraped hand. It thins and is gone. There's nothing else on the roof. The cat's ears come up off his skull one at a time.

Somewhere down the passage a sleeper thumps the wall twice with a fist and mutters something about slates and cats. Then the inn goes quiet again.

The shutters are still fastened, and the basin still sits under them, untouched. Outside, past the casement, whatever the man dropped lies in the gutter at the edge of the lean-to roof, about six feet below the sill.

 *(Out of game: the first action needed no roll. You were crossing your own room in Boots of Elvenkind and then speaking aloud, so staying quiet didn't matter once you announced yourself. The second action, the challenge, landed: he pulled the blade out and backed off. The one uncertain part was "Who sent you?", so I'll roll that now as Intimidation against a frightened man on a roof.)*

Your voice reaches him, and it frightens him enough to back off. It doesn't frighten him into talking. He bites off "nobody said nothing about..." before a name can follow, and fear of whoever sent him outweighs his fear of you. He runs without answering, and you learn nothing about who sent him.

*(Out of game: the card added +2 instead of your sheet's Intimidation +7. With the right bonus it's 4 + 7 = 11 against 15, so it's still a failure, and the result stands.)*
