The sergeant's quill keeps moving while you talk. He looks up once, at the cloak more than your face, takes in the faded regimental cut, and goes back to the page.

"Worgen." He spells it to himself under his breath and gets it right the first time. "Tethyr. Amn. Work, bed, roof." The nib scratches. "Fist's hiring. Fist is always hiring. Recruiting table's at the Seatower, out on the harbour, from first bell to noon. Tell them you can hold a line and they'll hand you a tabard. Pay's about two months behind, so don't spend it before you see it." He blots the line with the side of his ink-stained thumb. "Road work, try the Friendly Arm, a day south on the Trade Way. Caravans keep going missing past Beregost and the merchants are fighting over who pays for guards. That's honest work. Not much else round here is, and the honest stuff doesn't pay well." He turns the ledger slightly so the light falls on it. "Where're you sleeping? I need it written down."

The porter answers before you can, already shrugging your pack up onto one shoulder like it weighs nothing.

"Elfsong Tavern, Sergeant. Up Windspell Street." Then, to you, walking alongside: "That's the decent one. Clean sheets, and the lock on the door actually locks. There's a dead elf who sings at night, but she's never hurt anyone and some people pay extra for her. The cheap one would've been the Blushing Mermaid, right here on the quay, and you'd wake up without your boots. Tamsin Kell, by the way. You pay when we get to the door, not before. I'm honest, I'm just not stupid."

Vask writes *Elfsong* in a tired, square hand. "Next."

You step aside to let the line move. That brings the crates into view at the edge of your sight, and the lantern over the barrel. In the moment you weren't watching him, Copper got down off his bollard. Now he's sitting on the empty stool, tail wrapped round his paws, every bit of him facing the dealer's hands. Windspell Street runs downhill into the smell of the harbour. The milk cart has moved on and a bakehouse boy is sluicing his step. Copper goes ahead with his tail up, stops at every corner and waits, then goes on. At the bottom the quay opens out, grey water on the right and the Gull Steps behind. Mirela's barrel is empty at this hour, and the crates stand around it like furniture in a shut room. James turns left.

The fish market comes before he sees it, as Bram said it would. There are gutting tables under canvas, women with knives working faster than talk, and gulls lined along a ridgepole waiting for a mistake. Copper slows here, which is the closest he comes to a vice. He doesn't stop. Past the market the ropewalks begin: long, low sheds, each one longer than a ship, with their doors open on lines of hemp stretched taut down the whole length. Men walk backward down them, twisting strands as they go. The air is thick with tar. Nobody calls out to James, though a man at a shed door sharpening a hook stops, watches the cloak go by, and goes back to his hook when it has passed.

Rope Street climbs behind the sheds, narrow and steep, with washing strung across it from window to window, so walking up it is like walking under a row of flags. The houses are old and lean on each other. A pump stands halfway up. On a step near the bottom a boy of about twelve sits whittling a peg, and he isn't really watching the peg.

The first woman James comes to is broad and red-armed. She has pegs in her mouth and a wet sheet in both fists, and she's reaching for the line. She sees the hat come off and takes the pegs out of her mouth one at a time.

"Nettle's." She looks at the cloak, then at the cat sitting in the gutter, then back at him. "You're the first that's come asking with his hat off. The Fist don't come at all." She pegs the sheet with two quick jabs. "Up past the pump, on the left. There's a coil of old cable nailed over the door. Her husband put it there when he still had the walk at Corley's." She wipes her hands on her apron. "Go gently. She's had nobody tell her anything for nine days, and she's started answering the door like it's going to bite."

Behind him, down the street, the whittling stops. When James glances back, the step is empty and a shed door at the bottom is swinging shut.

The Nettle house is the narrowest on the street. A loop of grey, tarred cable, thick as a man's wrist, is nailed above the lintel and gone stiff with years of weather. The step is scrubbed. In the one front window, behind glass gone wavy with age, a thick candle burns low in a saucer. Its sides are pale yellow wax, and close to the base someone has pressed a small round stamp into it with a thumb: a coin with a woman's face on it.

Copper sits down on the scrubbed step without being asked and wraps his tail round his feet.

James knocks and steps back a pace.

For a while nothing happens. Then there's a scrape inside, a stool pushed back, and the door opens about as far as a hand is wide. The woman behind it is small and grey. Her hands are brown with tar to the wrists, and she holds a splicing fid in one of them like something she forgot to put down. She looks at the cloak first, the way everyone does, and her face tightens. She opens the door a little wider when she sees it isn't a Fist tabard. Then she sees the cat on her step. Then she looks at him.

"You're not Fist." Her voice is thin and very steady, the voice of someone who has practised staying steady. "And you're not from the Seatower, they don't send anybody." Her hand closes harder on the fid. "Is it Jory? Have you seen him?"

"Nine days," she says at last. Her voice is as steady as it was before. "Four times I went out to that tower. The last time a boy in a tabard told me dockhands go off on ships all the time and I should go home and wait." She breathes in through her nose. "I knew. I've known since the third day. A body can know a thing and still need someone to come and say it."

She opens the door the rest of the way and steps back.

"Come in, then. Mind the coil."

The house is one room deep and two rooms tall, with a ladder to a loft. Rope is everywhere: coils on pegs, a half-finished splice across a sawhorse, the floor swept around a heap of grey cable ends. There's a hearth with a pot pushed to the side of it, two stools and a table scrubbed white. A man's jacket hangs on the peg nearest the door, too big for her, its elbows patched. She doesn't look at it. Copper comes in after James, stops on the threshold and sits looking at the candle in the window. He goes no nearer.

Maud puts the fid down on the table at last, as if she's only now noticed it in her hand, and sits on one stool. She points to the other with her chin.

"You asked what he did. I'll tell you, and then you'll tell me the rest of what that mate said." She folds her tarred hands together. "He loaded. Any hold that was paying. The Fennick gang mostly, under old Harl, who's a fair foreman. They pay their bit to the Guild every tenday like everyone does down here, so nobody breaks their heads." Her mouth tightens. "A lot of good it did him."

She looks at the table, not at James.

"Ten, eleven days back he came home pleased with himself. A man had stopped him at the Fennick gate. Not Harl. Not anyone from the gang. Jory said he talked like he came from over the bridge and he wasn't a dock man, his hands were too soft. He wanted a strong back for one night's loading off a lighter, and he'd pay three times the day rate. Half in hand." She lifts her chin toward the window. "It was a gold piece. Jory never held a gold piece in his life. He put it on this table and laughed at it."

Then she looks at the candle.

"I took that gold up the hill to the Lady's Hall the next morning, because I thought luck money should go back to the Lady. There's a side door where they sell candles to folk who won't be let in at the front. A young sister sold me that one. She said burn it till he's home." For the first time the steady voice slips, very slightly, and she puts it right. "He went out the next night. It was warm. Warm wind off the land, in this season, and him in his shirt-sleeves. He said he'd be back by the dawn bell with the other half."

She is quiet a moment. The candle in the saucer gutters and catches again.

"That's all I know." She looks straight at him across the white table. "Now you. Where have they put him?"

Place: The Nettle house · Time: Day 2 · morning

James sits on the stool. The hat goes on his knee, and he keeps his eyes off the peg by the door.

Maud listens the way she listened on the step: hands folded on the white table, eyes on his face. At *Kindly Wind* she doesn't react. At *a copper in their teeth* her thumb presses once into the back of her other hand, hard, and lets go. When he says *write it in a book*, she breathes out through her nose. It isn't a laugh, though it comes close to one.

"A book." She looks at the candle in the window, then back at him. "Four times I went, and nobody wrote anything. A sergeant with a cloak, though. They'd write for that."

She gets up without being asked. She puts the pot back over the fire because her hands want something to do, and she answers his question with her back to him.

"He told it at this table like a joke. That's how I remember it." She moves the pot an inch, then back again. "The man called him *lad* the whole time, like a gentleman would. Jory said he had a dock coat on, but new, with no tar on it anywhere and stiff at the elbows. And he smelled like a barber's. Lavender water, Jory said, and he made a face, so I knew he meant a lot of it." She turns round. "The lighter wasn't coming to the Fennick. It was coming to the Fishgut Stair, below where the big ships lie. After second bell, when the tide turned. Jory said nobody unloads at the Fishgut at that hour. Then he laughed and said for triple, who cares."

She stops. The steady voice stays steady, but it takes her longer to find the next part.

"He asked could Jory swim." Her hand finds the edge of the table. "Jory told him no. Rope-walk lads never learn, there's no call to. And the man said good. Said that was safer. Nobody goes over the side showing off." She looks straight at James. "Jory thought that was funny. I thought it was a strange thing to want in a man you're hiring to carry crates."

The fire catches under the pot. Copper hasn't moved from the threshold. He has stopped watching the candle and is watching Maud.

"I'll come." She says it as if it was settled a while ago. "But not this afternoon. Peg Arlow's man went into the water two winters back. She was sick and couldn't go out to the tower, and when she could, they told her the unclaimed go out on the cart on the tenth day, to the pit past Rivington, under lime. No stone. No name." She takes the man's jacket off the peg at last, holds it for a moment, and puts it back. She takes her own shawl from the next peg down. "I don't know when they found him. Nobody told me that either. It's nine days since he went out."

She stands at her own door with the shawl in her tarred hands.

"So I'm asking you, Sergeant. Will you take me now?"

Place: The Nettle house · Time: Day 2 · morning

James is on his feet before she finishes asking, and the hat goes back on his head. Maud looks at him for a moment as if she hadn't expected the answer to come so fast. Then she nods once and goes to the dresser by the hearth.

She doesn't take long. She comes back with two things and holds them out flat on her tarred palm so he can see them. One is a wooden pay tally the length of a finger, notched along one edge and burned at the end with a brand of a crude F inside a ring. The other is a folded square of paper, greasy at the corners. It's a wage chit, a tenday's pay in a slanting foreman's hand: *J. Nettle, 6 days, Fennick. H.*

"Harl's hand," she says. "He writes them for the ones who can't count it themselves. Jory could, but he kept them anyway." The tally and the chit go into the pocket of her apron, under the shawl. She glances at the candle in the window and leaves it burning.

At the door James stops and lets Copper go out first. The cat steps down onto the scrubbed step, looks both ways along the street like a man crossing a road, and waits. Maud comes out under James's arm, pulls the door shut behind her and turns the key. Then she stands for a moment with her hand flat on the wood.

"Beside," she says. "Not behind. I heard you." She puts her chin up. "His name, clear, once. I can do that."

They go down Rope Street together under the washing. She walks quickly for a small woman, and James doesn't have to slow much. Two doors down a curtain moves. At the pump, a woman filling a bucket stops pumping and watches them pass. She says nothing, but she touches two fingers to her own lips and then to her heart as Maud goes by. Maud gives her a short nod back.

James keeps his eyes on the bottom of the street. The step where the whittling boy sat is still empty. The shed door that swung shut behind him is open now.

A man is leaning in that doorway, in no hurry at all. He's lean and somewhere past forty, clean-shaven, in a good brown coat buttoned to the throat. The coat isn't new and isn't tarred, and it's the plain kind a clerk wears when he doesn't want to look like one. James can see no weapon on him, which only means he isn't showing one. The whittling boy sits on an upturned bucket just inside the shed behind him, still working at the same peg.

The man straightens off the doorframe as they come down the last stretch of slope. He doesn't step into their path, but he stands where they have to pass him.

He takes his hat off. He does it to Maud first.

"Mistress Nettle." His voice is quiet, a Lower City voice with the corners sanded off. "I was sorry to hear Jory hadn't come home. We all were."

Maud stops. Her hand goes into her apron pocket and closes on the tally. Her voice doesn't change at all.

"His bit went to you every tenday. Harl paid it Fifthday mornings, regular." She looks at him the way she looked at James through a hand's width of door. "You were sorry nine days ago too, then. Nobody came to say so."

The man takes that without blinking, the way someone takes a debt he knows is owed. He doesn't argue. He turns to James and puts his hat back on.

"Ser. Nobody's stopping you." He says it plainly, as a fact. "This is our street, though, and our men are the ones going in the water. So when a Tethyrian in a regimental cloak walks up it on his second morning in the city, asks for Jory Nettle's house by name, and walks out with Jory Nettle's mother in her good shawl, the people I answer to will want to know why." He keeps his hands where James can see them, loose at his sides. "I'd rather ask you than guess. What's your business with the Nettles, and where are you taking her?"

Copper has sat down on the cobbles exactly between James's boots and the man's. He's looking at the boy's peg, not at the man.

I sit on the stool she pointed at, and I put the hat on my knee, and I don't look at the jacket on the peg either.

"Straight, then. The mate — Teague — had the middle watch the night before they took your son out of the water. He won't say more than that, and I won't put words in his mouth. The Fist pulled a dockhand from the water off the Wide the next day. The dead-cart lads bring them up to the Seatower in the morning. That's where he'll be — or where he was. The porters say the drowned come out with a copper in their teeth, and the Fist says drink and writes nothing down."

I let her have that, and I keep my voice low. "I don't know why they've kept his name from you. I can think of reasons and none of them are kind. But I was a sergeant once, and the Fist still looks at a cloak like this before it looks at the face wearing it. I'll go out to the Seatower this afternoon and ask for him by name, as a man who served, and I'll make them write it in a book. If you want to come, you come with me. If you'd rather not stand in that tower a fifth time, I'll bring you back whatever they say, word for word."

Then, because I need it: "The soft-handed man from over the bridge. Did Jory say anything else about him — how he dressed, what he smelled of, which lighter, which quay? Anything a man would notice and a mother would remember him saying."

I'm on my feet before she's finished the question, hat back on my head.

"Yes. Now." I nod at the shawl. "Bring anything that says you're his mother — a pay chit, a letter, his name on paper from the Fennick gang if you've got one. Soldiers in tabards like paper. And leave the candle burning. The sister said till he's home."

At the door I stop and let Copper go out first, then hold it for her. "Walk beside me, not behind. I'll do the talking at the gate, and they'll look at the cloak before they look at either of us. When they ask, you say his name, clear, once. Then you let me be unpleasant about the book."

Down Rope Street I keep my pace to hers and keep an eye on the shed door at the bottom that swung shut behind the whittling boy. Then left along the quay, the water on our left this time, toward the Seatower.

**Player's note — James Worgen, session one**

**What worked.** The city. From the first message I believed the Gull Steps smelled of tar and river mud, and nothing afterwards broke that. The NPCs each had one true thing about them that made them more than furniture: Tamsin making change from my gold and being annoyed about it, Bram pushing two silvers back across the bar *twice* because he doesn't hold money against mutton, Teague talking to the bottles instead of to me, Maud's "a body can know a thing and still need someone to come and say it." That last line landed hard. The GM also knew when to shut up — the Nettle doorstep, the Elfsong song — and let silence do the work, which is rarer than it should be.

The restraint on the mystery was exactly right. Three wheels in a night, each slightly different, and no one explaining any of them. The GM honoured my choice not to turn the card instead of nudging me toward it, and Copper lying *beside* it rather than on it told me more than a speech would have. Seeing the singer through the cat's eyes — a hollow in the dust where someone sits with her knees drawn up — was the best single image of the session. And the world moved without me: Mirela coming to ask which room was mine, the whittling boy reporting up the chain, the Guild man waiting at the bottom of the street because I walked a Guild street with my hat off. Consequences arriving on their own schedule, as the campaign file promised.

I also appreciated the GM asking me about the letter rather than inventing it, and then weaving Dessa and Orlan in cleanly. Rolls came only when they mattered, and the advantage reasoning was always stated.

**What broke.** The skill-modifier bug, three times: the card displayed "Persuasion +7" and added +4; "Religion +3" and added +4. The GM caught it and ruled correctly each time, but it cost a turn of out-of-game back-and-forth on the first one, and the server still logged that check as a failure. That needs fixing at the source.

Twice an in-character action got swallowed: once when my "?" question was followed by "nothing was sent," and once when a full turn I'd written reached the GM through the out-of-game channel and had to be resent word for word. Minor, but it jars.

The out-of-game notes repeat themselves — the same paragraph about "none of those needed a roll" appeared twice in one reply, and the GM has a habit of summarising what it just narrated. I don't need that. Trust the prose.

Small record issues: the letter from the Lanterns was on my sheet but not in inventory until I pointed it out; the records say Healing Light is "up to 4 dice at once" while my sheet says 5. And the voice slid from second person ("you") in the opening to third person ("James") thereafter — pick one.

**What was missing.** Nothing I'd call a failing for a first session, but to flag for the future: no crew yet, no sense of what Tymora actually wants beyond the coin going warm and cold, and no fight — I don't need one, but I'd like to know the GM can run combat with the same care. The Counting House note is the obvious hinge and I'm glad it's waiting. I'd also like a little more texture on Copper when he's being a cat and not an instrument — he's at his best when he's slightly rude.

I'll be back for the Seatower. Bring the book.

Yes. Two, honestly.

The card. I wrote "I don't turn it over" and meant it, but that was James's restraint, not mine — I wanted to see the face as badly as he did. The GM made it worse in the best way: no crease on it after a month folded in four, Copper lying beside it, the coin going neither warm nor cold. Every signal said *this one matters* and nothing said *don't*. I held off because the goddess's ban is the one rule James has, and breaking it in a rented room with nobody watching felt like cheating the premise before the campaign had earned it. But if the GM had put one more small pressure on — Mirela at the door, say, or the chandler's stamp turning out to be a wheel — I think James turns it, and I'd have let him. I'm not sure I was right to wait. A weakness you never test isn't a weakness.

The other was smaller. When the singer finished and the dust started drifting again, I wanted to send Copper up into the rafters. Not me with a lantern — him, silent, to sit on that beam and see what a cat sees when there's no one there. I'd just promised Bram I wouldn't climb his beams, and it felt like the kind of promise a man like James keeps to the letter and breaks in spirit, which is exactly the move I didn't want to make on the first night with a goddess watching. So I didn't. But the cat flattened his fur like he'd been *recognised*, and I walked away from that. I'll be thinking about it until the next session.

And a half-one: Bram said "walk it like you've been asked," and I chose to be seen on Rope Street — hat off, cloak on, a man with somewhere to be — when Mask of Many Faces was right there and I could have gone in as a ropemaker's cousin. That one I'd do again. The Guild man waiting at the bottom of the street is a conversation I want to have. But I noticed myself choosing the hard road because it made a better scene rather than because James would, and that's worth watching.

turns.message:
I step up to the trestle table, keeping my eyes on the sergeant and off that face-down hand between the crates. "James Worgen. Come down from the south — Tethyr, by way of Amn. Looking for honest work, a bed, and a roof that doesn't leak. How long I stay depends on how fast I find the first two." I glance at the ink on his thumb and add, soldier to soldier, "Ser-geant, if the Fist's hiring or someone's paying for road work, I'd take a name."

Then to the porter, without turning: "Decent one. Two silvers — and you tell me which is which."
turns.reply:
The sergeant's quill keeps moving while you talk. He looks up once, at the cloak more than your face, takes in the faded regimental cut, and goes back to the page.

"Worgen." He spells it to himself under his breath and gets it right the first time. "Tethyr. Amn. Work, bed, roof." The nib scratches. "Fist's hiring. Fist is always hiring. Recruiting table's at the Seatower, out on the harbour, from first bell to noon. Tell them you can hold a line and they'll hand you a tabard. Pay's about two months behind, so don't spend it before you see it." He blots the line with the side of his ink-stained thumb. "Road work, try the Friendly Arm, a day south on the Trade Way. Caravans keep going missing past Beregost and the merchants are fighting over who pays for guards. That's honest work. Not much else round here is, and the honest stuff doesn't pay well." He turns the ledger slightly so the light falls on it. "Where're you sleeping? I need it written down."

The porter answers before you can, already shrugging your pack up onto one shoulder like it weighs nothing.

"Elfsong Tavern, Sergeant. Up Windspell Street." Then, to you, walking alongside: "That's the decent one. Clean sheets, and the lock on the door actually locks. There's a dead elf who sings at night, but she's never hurt anyone and some people pay extra for her. The cheap one would've been the Blushing Mermaid, right here on the quay, and you'd wake up without your boots. Tamsin Kell, by the way. You pay when we get to the door, not before. I'm honest, I'm just not stupid."

Vask writes *Elfsong* in a tired, square hand. "Next."

You step aside to let the line move. That brings the crates into view at the edge of your sight, and the lantern over the barrel. In the moment you weren't watching him, Copper got down off his bollard. Now he's sitting on the empty stool, tail wrapped round his paws, every bit of him facing the dealer's hands. He's planted right over the face-down hand as if he'd paid for the seat.

One of the dockhands snorts. The tiefling doesn't laugh. She gives you that half-mouth smile, clicking her rings against the barrel-head one after another.

"Your cat's taken your seat, friend," she calls, quick and light. "That hand's dealt and paid for already. Someone's got to turn it over, and it isn't going to be him."

Tamsin stops one step up the street with your pack on her shoulder and waits to see which way you'll go.

Half a wheel, cut clean through the middle as if someone had taken a chisel to the hub.

The fourth card lands in front of the empty stool, face-down, and stays there. She's already dealing the seat again.

Copper's tail stays stiff the whole way up the steps.

Tamsin waits until the crates and the lantern are behind a warehouse corner and the street starts climbing. It's cobbled and narrow, with tavern noise spilling from doorways and a lamplighter working his way down the far side with a pole. She shifts the pack, glances at the cat, then at him.

"Cut through the hub?" She takes a few steps before she goes on, which for her is a long time. "Not a mark I know. It's not a guild's, not a house's. The patriar houses stamp their marks on everything, their barrels, their bales, their bloody gangplanks. I've hauled for half of them and I've never seen a wheel."

Two more steps.

"But you asked about a copper, so here's what I know about coppers. The drowned ones. The Fist fishes them out of the harbour, dockhands mostly, sometimes a porter, and every one of them has a copper in his teeth. Folk say it's fare for Umberlee. The dead-cart lads talk when they've had a drink. I never saw the face of one myself, so I can't tell you it's your wheel." She lowers her voice without slowing down. "Don't ask about it loud down on the quay, ser. Those dockhands pay the Guild to keep them safe, and the Guild hates being seen not doing it. The lamplighter's pole clicks against a bracket overhead. A flame catches.

turns.reply:
James reaches into his purse and finds only gold, the last hand's winnings, with no silver among it. Tamsin sees the yellow glint and sighs as if she'd been expecting it. She lowers the pack onto the step, digs into a pocket inside her coat and counts silver out by feel.

"Knew it. Southerners and their gold." She takes the gold piece, holds it up to the doorway light and puts seven silvers back in his hand. "There. Three's mine, the talking one too. I'm not proud."

When he mentions the dead-cart lads she glances once down the street, the way they came, before she answers.

"They do the morning run out of the Seatower and they're done drinking by noon. I can't ask them straight out, because they'll want to know why a porter cares." She tucks the silver away. "But they get chatty about a face on a coin. If I hear, you'll hear. If you've moved on, I'll find out where. Finding people's half my trade, ser."

Then she's gone down Windspell Street at a porter's trot, light without the pack, and the lamplighter's flame sways behind her.

The door opens on warmth. The Elfsong's common room is low and long, with dark beams overhead. A fire burns at the far end. Tables are full of people who look like they have somewhere to sleep: clerks, a pair of caravan masters arguing over a map, a halfling family eating together. Copper drops off James's shoulder and pads in ahead of him. He doesn't look at anyone. He walks straight under the nearest bench as though he's checking it's still there. Nobody is singing. A few people glance up at the ceiling now and then, the way you'd look at a clock.

A broadsheet of *Baldur's Mouth* is nailed to a post by the bar, a few days old and greasy at the corners. Most of it is about grain prices and some duke's speech. Near the bottom, in small type: *ANOTHER FOR UMBERLEE — dockhand taken from the water off the Wide, name withheld pending kin.*

The barman is broad and grey-bearded, with the forearms of a man who used to roll the barrels himself. He finishes wiping a mug before he looks at James.

"Room's eight silver a night, paid in the morning. Lock works and the window doesn't open onto anything you'd climb. Supper's three, paid when it lands. Mutton tonight, or there's fish if you trust it." He sets the mug down. "And the house red you're not to give the lady?" One corner of his beard lifts. "We call it Chionthar Rose. The regulars call it the Penance. I'd not give it to anyone I owed."

He pulls a slate from under the counter, chalk ready.

"A drink on your name, is it? What name, and what does she get instead?"

"That covers tonight's room, the mutton — I'll pass on the fish till I've seen what the harbour's giving back — and whatever she drinks that isn't the Penance. Tiefling woman, silver rings, deals cards down on the Gull Steps. Mirela. Put the best of what's left on the slate for her, and keep the change against tomorrow."

I take the mug he draws for me and lean an elbow on the bar, nodding at the greasy broadsheet on the post. "That's the second time tonight someone's told me about Umberlee collecting dockhands. You've stood behind this counter long enough to hear everything twice. The Fist calls it drink. What do the men who actually drink here call it?"
turns.reply:
Bram picks up the gold piece and turns it once under the lamp. He doesn't bite it.

"Worgen." The chalk squeaks on the slate: *WORGEN — for the dealer, M.* "That's ten silver. Supper's three. Her cup's two, Amnian red out of the cask I don't water. Your ale comes with the supper. That leaves five against the room, and the room's eight. You'll owe me three in the morning." He slides the coin under the counter. "I don't hold change against tomorrow. I hold it against what you've had."

He draws the ale, sets it down and listens to the question without looking at the broadsheet.

"Men who drink here aren't dockhands. Dockhands drink at the Mermaid, where it's cheaper and nobody minds the noise." He takes the next order, a jug for the caravan masters, and comes back. "I get the ships' mates, though, and the clerks who write up the cargoes. They don't call it drink."

He glances down the bar. A weathered man in a mate's coat is nursing something brown at the end of it, hat pulled low, and hasn't been listening.

"They say it's the wind. Some nights it gets up off the land with no weather behind it, warm when it ought to be cold. A ship goes out on it, and a day or so later there's a man in the water." He shrugs with one heavy shoulder. "Sailors will tell you any wind is somebody's. That's sailors. But they've stopped laughing about this one, and they don't say it loud. You'd not ask it loud either. Not in here. Not to men who have to sail on it."

The mutton comes through the kitchen hatch on a board: thick slices with the fat crackling, onions gone soft in the drippings, and a heel of dark bread. Bram puts it in front of James and takes no money for it, since it's paid for.

Under the bench behind James, Copper has arranged himself so that he can see the door. The fire pops. A few heads at the tables lift toward the dark beams and come down again. She still hasn't started.

turns.message:
I take the board and the ale and don't say anything more about the wind at the bar. I eat the mutton like a man who hasn't had hot fat in three days, mopping the drippings with the bread, and let the room settle round me.

When the board's clean I catch Bram's eye, tap the edge of the mate's brown cup with one finger, and put two silvers down. "Whatever he's having, from me. No reason on it." Then I take my ale down to the end of the bar and settle onto the stool one over from him — not next to, one over — with my back half to the room and my voice low enough for a ship's deck.

"I'm not asking about anything, ser. I came up from Amn on the *Gull*, and I'd like to know which ships I shouldn't go back down on. That's all. A man who sails can tell a man who doesn't which bottoms to avoid, and I'll take it as a kindness and forget where I heard it."
turns.reply:
James eats like a man who has lived three days on ship's biscuit and salt cod. The mutton's fat cracks between his teeth and the onions fall apart on the bread. He wipes the drippings up with the dark heel until the board shines. Under the bench, Copper accepts one strip of fat dropped without comment and keeps his eyes on the door.

The room gets used to him. The caravan masters go back to their map. The halfling father falls asleep sitting up, and his children steal his crust.

When the board is clean, James catches Bram's eye. He taps the rim of the mate's cup with one finger and puts two silvers on the counter. Bram looks at the coins, then at the cup, and doesn't ask. He takes down a squat bottle from the second shelf, the one the mate's drink came from, and fills a fresh cup with something the colour of old varnish. He sets it at the end of the bar, a hand's width from the mate's elbow. "Paid," he says, and goes back to his jugs.

James carries his ale down and takes the stool one over from the mate. He sits with his back half to the room and speaks in a deck voice.

The mate doesn't turn his head. He looks at the new cup for a long breath, the way you'd look at a rope someone else has coiled.

The mate puts two fingers on the new cup and draws it in, and leaves his old one where it stands.

"Off the *Gull*." His voice is dry, a man who has spent too long shouting into wind. "Ruel's old tub. You'll live on her. She's too poor to be worth anything to anybody." He drinks, holds it in his mouth a moment, swallows. "Kind of you. I'll take it as kind."

He still doesn't look round. He talks to the shelf of bottles.

"You've got the question the wrong way round, though. Ships that founder, anybody can tell you about them. Rotten seams, a drunk master, a hold loaded heavy on one side. You can see that from the quay." He turns the cup a quarter on the wood. "Keep off the ones that never lose anything."

The fire pops at the far end of the room. He waits for the noise to cover him.

"Ammerhal's ships. Swallowtail pennant, blue over white. The *Kindly Wind*'s the big one. She's lying off the Wide now. I've been in and out of this harbour six years, and in six years House Ammerhal hasn't lost a barrel. Not a cask stove in, not a bale gone wet. Three or four other houses fly a little blue ribbon under their own colours now, alongside her. I'll not name them in a room full of clerks." He drinks again. "They go out at night, on that wind Bram's been telling you about. Yes, I heard. It comes off the land warm with no weather behind it, and only their sails ever catch it. By the time anybody else has cast off, it's gone."

He sets the cup down very carefully.

"The dockhand they printed off the Wide. *Name withheld pending kin.*" His mouth moves without becoming a smile. "Jory Nettle. He loaded our hold, *Saltwife*'s, two days before. His kin is his mother on Rope Street, and she's been out to the Seatower four times asking for him. That's how *pending* they are." He finally turns his head, enough for James to see a lined face, a broken nose healed crooked, and eyes that have slept badly. "The night before they pulled Jory out, I had the middle watch. The wind came off the land warm. The *Kindly Wind* cleared the mole a little after the second bell past midnight, with every stitch she had set and no lamps on her."

He looks back at the bottles.

"I'm not saying anything by that. I'm saying I had the watch." He pushes the empty old cup an inch towards Bram's side of the bar. "Teague. Mate of the *Saltwife*. We go out on the morning tide on an honest land breeze, if one turns up. You'd do well not to sail on anything flying blue and white. And you never heard that from me, not even if somebody asks you kindly."

Above them, something changes in the room before there's any sound. The talk at the tables thins out. The halfling children stop squabbling over the crust. Bram puts down the jug he's holding.

Then, from somewhere among the dark beams, a woman's voice begins to sing in Elvish. It's very low and very clear, a slow line that rises and doesn't come down where you expect. Nobody looks for her. Most of the room bows its head the way people do at a graveside.

Teague closes his eyes and listens with the cup in both hands.

Under the bench, Copper has turned away from the door. He's looking up into the rafters, ears flat forward, and his fur is standing along his spine.

The room tips downward and goes thin. The colours drain to greys and dull golds, and the edges sharpen until every beam overhead is clear down to the grain and the old adze marks. The smells come in one after another: tallow, wet wool, hops, mutton fat, the halfling children's sticky hands. Then there's a smell that isn't one. Up between the third and fourth beams from the fire there's a patch of nothing, as clean and cold as a cellar, and the lamp-smoke curls away from it.

Copper's ears tell James exactly where the voice comes from, which human ears can't. The song isn't spread through the rafters. It comes from that one spot.

Warm air rises from the lamps and carries dust up through the room, and everywhere else the dust drifts. In that patch it hangs still. It forms a hollow about the size of someone sitting on the beam with her knees drawn up, and if a person's breath moves the air there, it doesn't move the dust.

The line climbs to the note that never comes down where you expect. On it the stillness up there seems to shift, as though whoever sits in it has looked down.

Something comes back through the bond, and it isn't alarm. The nearest thing to it is a cat on a wall being spotted by someone it used to know. Copper's fur flattens under James's hand from the shoulders down, all at once.

The note fades. The dust starts drifting again and the clean cold patch fills with smoke like any other bit of air. James is back behind his own eyes, crouched by a bench in a tavern that smells of mutton. Copper blinks once, slowly, and starts washing a paw as if nothing had happened.

Around the room heads come up. Someone lets out a breath. The halfling father wakes, and his children pretend they never touched his crust. Bram picks up the jug he'd put down.

At the bar, Teague opens his eyes and finds the stool beside him empty. When James straightens and gives him a nod, the mate lifts two fingers off his cup and puts them back. That's all the goodnight he gives, and he goes back to the bottles.

The Lady's coin is still warm against James's chest. It's cooling slowly, the way a stone does when someone has been sitting on it.

I sit on the bed and take out my papers. I haven't looked at the promissory note properly since that night — I was too busy being alive. Bram watches the five silvers land and takes three. He pushes the other two back across the wood with one thick finger.

"Room's square." He wipes the place where they lay. "Mutton gets paid when it lands. You'd want it back if you went under a cart before supper." He turns to the next jug, and then, without looking round: "Glad you won't climb them."

The stairs are narrow and worn into a dip in the middle of each tread. Copper goes up them ahead of James, as he always does. Room 4 is second on the right, the key turns stiffly, and the door is good oak with a lock that throws a real bolt. James tries it twice, and it holds both times.

The room has a bed, a washstand, a stool and one shuttered window. Copper goes round all four walls before he lets himself be in a room, nose low along the skirting, and finishes under the bed. James sets the lantern on the floorboards, turned down to a low yellow glow that won't put his shadow on the shutter.

The window looks down on the yard. Fifteen feet below are wet cobbles, a well with a lid on it, and the back door of the stable with a lantern hanging beside it. There's no ledge under the sill and no drainpipe within reach. Bram told the truth: nobody would climb it, and nobody would come up it without a ladder and a lot of noise. Across the yard an eight-foot wall cuts it off from the back of a chandler's shop. All its windows are dark but one on the upper floor, where a lamp burns behind a cheap curtain. The shutter bolts with an iron bar in a staple. The staple is a little loose in the wood, but it would take a crowbar to work it free. Down in the common room someone laughs, and the singer stays quiet.

James sits on the bed and takes out his papers. Under the regimental pay slip, folded in four and soft at the creases from a long road, is the note.

He remembers the man better than he remembered the paper. He was thin and had a Gate accent. There was ink worn into the cuffs of a good coat, and he kept doubling his bets in a way that showed he'd stopped counting. When the last hand turned he had no coin left, so he wrote this at the table. He was gone before dawn.

In the lantern light the note says, in a careful clerk's hand:

*The Counting House of Baldur's Gate will pay to the bearer on presentation the sum of three hundred gold pieces, drawn against the account styled* Fair Wind. *Payable at the Strongroom Wicket only, in person, before the evening chime.*

Below that is a signature: *Edric Vael, factor.*

Beside the signature someone has pressed a small seal into the paper with no wax, so it shows only as a raised shape when the light rakes across it. *Burn*

Copper comes out from under the bed. He doesn't look at the paper. He sits on the floor by the lantern and looks at the door.

The Lanterns, we called ourselves, because we did more work underground than any of us liked. Orlan Pell carried this rod ahead of us into the Nashkel dark and didn't carry it out, and I read one page of what came after and folded it away because I'd rather have lost a hand of cards than owed anyone anything.

James sets the promissory note face down on the blanket with its seal against the wool, and unfolds the letter.

It's thicker than he remembered: three sheets, folded in four together, the outer one worn soft from riding in his papers since the south. Dessa's hand runs across the outside in letters a finger tall: *J. WORGEN, by whoever's going his way*. Inside the lines are smaller but just as heavy, pressed hard enough to dent the paper, the hand of a woman who wrote standing up.

The first page is the one he has read before. He finds the place where he stopped, about two-thirds of the way down, where the ink is a little blotted:

*…and we buried him on the slope above the Nashkel workings, facing south because he always complained about the cold. Hask cut the marker. It's crooked. Orlan would have said so.*

*The rod came out in your hand, Jamie. You know that. You also walked off the road at Nashkel before any of us could say anything, so I'm saying it now. Orlan wanted you to have it. He said so in the dark, before the second fall, when he still thought we'd all get out. He said it to me, not you, because he knew what your face would do.*

That's where he folded it last time. The second page goes on in the same heavy hand:

*He also said this, and I'm writing it down word for word because he made me repeat it back to him:*

*"Tell Jamie the rod's paid for. He'll want to pay for it. Don't let him."*

*So that's settled. You don't owe him and you don't owe us. I know you, so I know you'll carry it around anyway like a stone in your boot. Put it down.*

*The share's been split. Yours is with the moneylender Ferrant in Athkatla under your name, and he'll hold it a year. Then it goes to Orlan's mother in Crimmor, because I'm not having it sit in a moneylender's box forever. If you've already lost the rest at some table, at least that much will be somewhere useful.*

The third page is shorter, and it's written in a different ink, as if she came back to it another day.

*One more thing, and I didn't know whether to send it.*

*This was in Orlan's coat, in the oilskin with his letters home. None of us has seen a deck like it. Wren says it's old, older than anything we brought out of that mine. Orlan never played, you know that, he wouldn't even dice for first watch. I don't know why he had it.*

*I didn't turn it over. You'll laugh. After the mine none of us wanted to know anything we didn't have to. You can decide. You were always the one who could look at a card and not need to know what it was.*

*We're wintering in Athkatla. If you ever want to owe somebody something, it can be me.*

*— D.*

Folded into the last fold of the third sheet, where the paper doubles over on itself, is a card.

James has carried this letter folded in four, under a pay slip, through Amn and up the coast on a ship. The creases cross the third sheet in both directions, and the card was sitting in the middle of them. It has no crease at all. It lies on the paper perfectly flat, and its corners are still sharp, as if the folds had gone around it.

It came out face down, the way Dessa said.

The back is vellum rather than pasteboard, gone the colour of weak tea, with gilt worn away at the edges where thumbs once held it. A wheel is painted on it, filling the card nearly to the border: eight spokes, a rim, and a hub. The hub is whole.

That's the third wheel James has seen tonight. On the quay there was half a spoked wheel on a dull copper coin, cut through the hub. On the note there's a toothed wheel like a mill gear, pressed blind into the paper. And now this one, unbroken.

The lantern on the floor burns steadily. Under his shirt the Lady's coin is neither warm nor cold, only the heat of his own skin.

Copper turns his head from the door.

He gets up and crosses the floorboards without hurrying, then puts his nose to the edge of the card without touching it. He sniffs it for a long moment, the way he went round the skirting when they came in. Then he lies down on the blanket right beside it, flank against the paper, not on top of it. He tucks his paws under himself and looks back at the door.

The card lies between James's knee and the cat, wheel up.

turns.message:
I don't turn it over.

I look at it a long time, the wheel side up, and my thumb wants it — wants it badly, the way it's wanted every card for three tendays. Dessa's right: I was always the one who could look at a card and not need to know. That was before I needed to know everything. So I put my hands flat on my knees and leave it lying there between Copper and me, and I take the Lady's coin out from under my shirt and lay it on the blanket beside the card instead, her worn profile next to the whole wheel. "Three wheels in one night, Lady. One cut through, one with teeth, one whole. If this is the lesson, I'm listening. I just don't know the alphabet yet."

Then I do what a soldier does with a thing he doesn't understand: I try to remember where I've seen it before. The toothed wheel I've seen on Gond's priests, and on half the counting-house doors in Athkatla. The spoked wheel — I turn it over in my head: temple carvings, the cards the Calishite dealers use, the old Tethyrian decks, anything Orlan ever muttered over a fire about wheels and luck and the goddess who turns them. I dig for it.
turns.reply:
James leaves the card where it lies. His thumb wants it. It moves a hair's width toward the gilt edge, and he presses both hands flat on his knees to stop it.

He draws the Lady's coin out on its cord and lays it on the blanket beside the card. Her worn profile sits next to the whole wheel. In the low lantern light the two look about the same age.

Copper watches the coin come down. He doesn't move.

The toothed wheel he doesn't need to dig for. Every soldier who has guarded a paymaster's chest knows that mark. It's Gond's cog, the Wonderbringer's sign. The god's artificers stamp it on the locks, hinges and strongbox fittings they build. In Athkatla you saw it over the counting-house doors, cut into the iron, where it told thieves which locks a priest of Gond had made and warned them not to waste the night. So a blind Gondar seal beside a factor's signature doesn't stand for any family. It's the mark of the lock.

The spoked wheel is harder. James goes looking for it: carvings in temples he only passed through, Calishite decks with suits nobody in the north plays, the old Tethyrian cards with crowned queens. And Orlan by the fire, who never played but always had something to say about the goddess the rest of them were praying to under their breath.

He doesn't find it.

He gets pieces, but they don't fit together. An old Calishite deck had a wheel as the one card with no suit, and the dealers set it aside before a game. He never asked why. A carving over a shrine door somewhere on the road through Amn had been chiselled half away, but he couldn't say whose shrine it was or who had done the chiselling. And Orlan said something once, at a fire above some river crossing, with his boots steaming. James can hear the tone more clearly than the words: half a joke, the voice a man uses when he's repeating something his grandmother told him. *The wheel, Jamie. It used to be* —

The fire popped, someone laughed, and the rest is gone. Whatever Orlan meant to say, James was too busy dealing to listen. He was dealing then.

He sits with that for a while.

The coin and the card lie side by side on the blanket. The Lady's coin stays at the warmth of his skin, no warmer. The wheel on the vellum stays exactly as painted, eight spokes and a whole hub.

Copper shifts on the blanket. He doesn't move off the card. He stretches out one front paw until it rests, very lightly, on the cord of the Lady's coin, and he leaves it there. Then he looks back at the door.

Downstairs someone drops a mug and Bram says one short word. The lantern burns low and steady on the floor. Across the yard, the chandler's upper window is still lit.

James lets his breath out. "Not tonight, then."

The card goes back into the third sheet exactly as Dessa sent it, wheel up and face down. He tucks the letter under the pay slip and lays the pay slip over the note, then puts the whole bundle inside his coat, where it rides against his ribs. When he lifts the Lady's coin by its cord, Copper's paw comes off it without fuss. The coin goes back under his shirt and settles against his skin.

He turns the lantern down until the wick is a red thread and then nothing. The room goes black. He gives his eyes a minute, and the dark gets thinner: a grey seam around the shutter, the pale shape of the washstand. Copper stays a darker lump on the blanket with his eyes half-lit.

The bar comes up out of its staple slowly, and the loose staple barely clicks. He opens the shutter a finger's width.

The yard is the same as before: wet cobbles, the lidded well, the stable lantern burning low by its door. Across it, above the eight-foot wall, the chandler's upper window is still lit. The cheap curtain is thin enough to show what's behind it. A lamp hangs from a hook, and under it an old man in shirtsleeves works at a dipping frame. He lowers a row of wicks into a vat, lifts them out, waits, and lowers them again. Racks of finished tapers hang behind him in rows like organ pipes. On the bench by his elbow a short stack of thicker candles stands apart from the rest. He picks one up, presses something small into its side with his thumb, the way a clerk stamps wax, and sets it down. At this distance James can't make out the stamp. A boy is asleep on a sack in the corner with one arm over his face.

James watches for his minute. The curtain moves only when the heat from the vat lifts it. The old man never looks up from his wicks, and never looks across at the Elfsong. He's a man working through the night for an order due in the morning, and nothing about him suggests he's watching anyone.

The bar goes back into its staple. James props the rapier against the bedframe where his hand will find it and slides the rod under the bolster. Copper waits until he's lying down, then walks up the blanket and settles against the coat, on the side where the papers are. He purrs once, briefly, the way he does when he's decided something, and goes quiet.

The night passes without trouble. Downstairs the common room empties a little at a time, with chairs scraping and Bram's bar coming down across the front door. Nobody sings again. Once, deep in the small hours, a step comes along the corridor and goes on past room 4 without slowing, and a door further down opens and shuts. Copper lifts his head for it, then puts it down again.

James wakes to grey light at the shutter's edge and the harbour bells ringing the turn of the tide. Somewhere below the Elfsong's roofline, ships are going out on the morning water. The chandler's window across the yard is dark now. Copper is sitting up on the coat, washing behind one ear, and he looks like he has been awake for hours.

The common room looks different in the morning. The shutters are open on a grey yard, the fire is down to coals someone is building back up, and the long tables are mostly bare boards. One caravan master eats alone with his map folded beside the plate. At the end of the bar, Teague's stool is empty and his cup has been cleared away. Out past the roofs, the tide bells have stopped.

James takes the end nearest the kitchen hatch. Copper doesn't go under a bench this time. He sits on the floor by James's boot, facing the door.

Bram finishes wiping a mug before he looks up. "Hot's fried bread, bacon and two eggs, with small beer. Two silver." He calls it through the hatch, and the pan answers him.

While it cooks, James asks his question in a voice for asking directions. Bram hears it all out without stopping his hands.

"Counting House is three streets toward the water and one east. Grey stone, bars on the lower windows. It's the one building down there with no beggars on its step." He sets the mug on the shelf. "I bank the house takings in the front hall: clerks at benches, deposits, letters of credit. The Wicket's at the back, down a stair. There's a grille in an iron door, and it opens after noon and shuts at the evening chime. I've never stood at it. The clerks who drink here say it pays out on the sealed accounts, the ones that don't want their names over a door."

He takes a jug from a girl coming through from the cellar and sends her back for another.

"Do they take a stranger's paper across the counter? No. They look at you first. Then they check the paper against their book, and if the sum's big they send a runner to whoever keeps the account, and you wait on a bench while he goes. They'll write down your name and where you sleep." He glances at the floor where Copper sits. "That part you'd already know, if you'd been on the Gull Steps last night."

James turns the mug a quarter on the wood. One corner of Bram's beard lifts. He doesn't comment on it.

"Vael." He says the name as if testing the weight. "If a man's drunk under my beams, I don't give his name to the next man who asks. Same as I'd not give out yours." He leaves it there. "*Fair Wind*, now. That's no house's name. A patriar house puts its own name on its money. When a few of them go in together on something, they give the account a name like that so none of theirs is on it. The clerks say it's for luck. Mostly it's so you can't tell who's in it."

The plate comes through the hatch: the bacon crisp at the edges, the eggs still trembling, the bread black-gold from the fat. Bram puts it down and takes the two silvers off the wood when James lays them there.

"Your dealer came in for her cup," he adds, as if the plate reminded him. "Near when I put the bar across. Tiefling, rings. Drank the red standing up, didn't sit. She asked which room was yours." He puts the coins in the till. "I told her the Elfsong has rooms."

He nods at the pack on James's shoulder.

"You're carrying that like you're going somewhere. Room 4 another night, or is that key coming back to me?"

I finish the small beer and shrug the pack back on. "The Wicket doesn't open till noon, you said. Then I'll spend the morning on the other errand." I don't say which. "Rope Street — that's down toward the harbour, the rope-walks? A left or a right off the quay?"

Copper's already at the door.
turns.reply:
Bram finishes wiping a mug before he picks up the gold piece. He doesn't turn it under the lamp this time.

"Room's paid in the morning. You're paying a morning early." He drops it under the counter and counts silver out onto the wood. "Eight for tonight. And you'd know by now I don't hold the other two against mutton you haven't eaten." He slides two silvers back toward the plate, the same way he did last night. One corner of his beard lifts. "Pay me when it lands."

When James mentions the dealer, Bram stops with the cloth in his hand and looks at him properly for the first time this morning.

"Tiefling, rings. If she asks, she gets *four*." The cloth goes back to work. "Anyone else gets what she got last night. That's what they'd get anyway."

He watches the pack go back onto James's shoulder, then the cat already sitting at the door with his tail curled round his paws, looking at the latch as if it owes him money.

"Rope Street." Bram points with his chin toward the water, through the wall. "Down Windspell to the quay. At the bottom you turn left, with the water on your right. Keep along past the fish market. You'll smell it before you see it. After that come the long sheds, the ropewalks, a cable's length of them. Rope Street runs behind the sheds, up the slope. Narrow, washing across it, the ropemakers' widows mostly." He takes an empty jug from the girl coming up from the cellar. "Guild streets, down there. Folk notice who walks them. Walk it like you've been asked."

He turns away to the caravan master, who wants more small beer.

Outside, the morning is grey and damp, and the street is starting to fill: a milk cart, two clerks with ink-boxes under their arms, a boy hosing down the step of the bakehouse opposite. Down the slope, where the roofs drop away, a strip of harbour shows between two chimneys, the colour of slate. Copper waits on the Elfsong's step until James's boot is over the threshold, then goes ahead of him, as he always does.

turns.message:
I go down Windspell with Copper ahead of me, left at the bottom with the water on my right, and past the fish market without hurrying — a soldier's walk, not a scout's. I let the ropewalks come up on me, the long sheds and the smell of tar and hemp, and I keep my eyes on the street, not the doorways. Bram's right: people notice who walks these streets. So I let them notice a man in a Tethyrian cloak who has somewhere to be.

Behind the sheds, on Rope Street, I stop at the first woman hanging washing and take my hat off. "Mistress — I'm looking for the Nettle house. Jory's mother. I was sent by a man off a ship he loaded, who thought someone should come." Which is true, near enough.

When I find her door I knock, step back a pace so I'm not looming, and let her see the cloak and the cat before I say anything.
turns.reply:
Windspell Street runs downhill into the smell of the harbour. The milk cart has moved on and a bakehouse boy is sluicing his step. Copper goes ahead with his tail up, stops at every corner and waits, then goes on. At the bottom the quay opens out, grey water on the right and the Gull Steps behind. Mirela's barrel is empty at this hour, and the crates stand around it like furniture in a shut room. James turns left.

The fish market comes before he sees it, as Bram said it would. There are gutting tables under canvas, women with knives working faster than talk, and gulls lined along a ridgepole waiting for a mistake. Copper slows here, which is the closest he comes to a vice. He doesn't stop. Past the market the ropewalks begin: long, low sheds, each one longer than a ship, with their doors open on lines of hemp stretched taut down the whole length. Men walk backward down them, twisting strands as they go. The air is thick with tar. Nobody calls out to James, though a man at a shed door sharpening a hook stops, watches the cloak go by, and goes back to his hook when it has passed.

Rope Street climbs behind the sheds, narrow and steep, with washing strung across it from window to window, so walking up it is like walking under a row of flags. The houses are old and lean on each other. A pump stands halfway up. On a step near the bottom a boy of about twelve sits whittling a peg, and he isn't really watching the peg.

The first woman James comes to is broad and red-armed. She has pegs in her mouth and a wet sheet in both fists, and she's reaching for the line. She sees the hat come off and takes the pegs out of her mouth one at a time.

"Nettle's." She looks at the cloak, then at the cat sitting in the gutter, then back at him. "You're the first that's come asking with his hat off. The Fist don't come at all." She pegs the sheet with two quick jabs. "Up past the pump, on the left. There's a coil of old cable nailed over the door. Her husband put it there when he still had the walk at Corley's." She wipes her hands on her apron. "Go gently. She's had nobody tell her anything for nine days, and she's started answering the door like it's going to bite."

Behind him, down the street, the whittling stops. When James glances back, the step is empty and a shed door at the bottom is swinging shut.

The Nettle house is the narrowest on the street. A loop of grey, tarred cable, thick as a man's wrist, is nailed above the lintel and gone stiff with years of weather. The step is scrubbed. In the one front window, behind glass gone wavy with age, a thick candle burns low in a saucer. Its sides are pale yellow wax, and close to the base someone has pressed a small round stamp into it with a thumb: a coin with a woman's face on it.

Copper sits down on the scrubbed step without being asked and wraps his tail round his feet.

James knocks and steps back a pace.

For a while nothing happens. Then there's a scrape inside, a stool pushed back, and the door opens about as far as a hand is wide. The woman behind it is small and grey. Her hands are brown with tar to the wrists, and she holds a splicing fid in one of them like something she forgot to put down. She looks at the cloak first, the way everyone does, and her face tightens. She opens the door a little wider when she sees it isn't a Fist tabard. Then she sees the cat on her step. Then she looks at him.

"You're not Fist." Her voice is thin and very steady, the voice of someone who has practised staying steady. "And you're not from the Seatower, they don't send anybody." Her hand closes harder on the fid. "Is it Jory? Have you seen him?"

turns.message:
I take the hat fully off and hold it in both hands, and I don't step forward. I've stood at doors like this before, in Tethyr, with a sergeant's list in my pocket. There's no good way. There's only the straight one.

"Mistress Nettle. My name is James Worgen. I haven't seen him. I'm not going to tell you I have." I keep my voice low and level, for her and not for the street. "But I sat last night with the mate of the *Saltwife* — the ship Jory loaded, two days before. He's a decent man and he's not sleeping. He told me the Fist took a dockhand out of the water off the Wide, and that the *Mouth* printed it without a name. He believes it was your son. I believe him. That's why I'm on your step with my hat off instead of the Seatower sending nobody."

I let that land. I don't fill the silence.

Then, quieter: "I don't know why they haven't told you. I'd like to find out. If you'll let me in and sit a moment, I'll tell you everything I was told, and you can tell me about Jory — where he worked, who he worked for, whether he ever brought home anything that wasn't wages." My eyes go, just once, to the candle in the window with the Lady's face pressed into its side. "And who sold you that."
turns.reply:
Maud doesn't move while he speaks. She stands in the hand's-width gap with the fid in her fist and her eyes on his face, never on the hat, never on the cat. When he says *off the Wide* her hand closes on the fid until the knuckles go pale under the tar. Nothing else about her changes.

He doesn't fill the silence, and she doesn't either. Down the street a shutter bangs. Somewhere behind the sheds a man shouts a count, and the ropewalk answers with a long creak of hemp coming taut.

"Nine days," she says at last. Her voice is as steady as it was before. "Four times I went out to that tower. The last time a boy in a tabard told me dockhands go off on ships all the time and I should go home and wait." She breathes in through her nose. "I knew. I've known since the third day. A body can know a thing and still need someone to come and say it."

She opens the door the rest of the way and steps back.

"Come in, then. Mind the coil."

The house is one room deep and two rooms tall, with a ladder to a loft. Rope is everywhere: coils on pegs, a half-finished splice across a sawhorse, the floor swept around a heap of grey cable ends. There's a hearth with a pot pushed to the side of it, two stools and a table scrubbed white. A man's jacket hangs on the peg nearest the door, too big for her, its elbows patched. She doesn't look at it. Copper comes in after James, stops on the threshold and sits looking at the candle in the window. He goes no nearer.

Maud puts the fid down on the table at last, as if she's only now noticed it in her hand, and sits on one stool. She points to the other with her chin.

"You asked what he did. I'll tell you, and then you'll tell me the rest of what that mate said." She folds her tarred hands together. "He loaded. Any hold that was paying. The Fennick gang mostly, under old Harl, who's a fair foreman. They pay their bit to the Guild every tenday like everyone does down here, so nobody breaks their heads." Her mouth tightens. "A lot of good it did him."

She looks at the table, not at James.

"Ten, eleven days back he came home pleased with himself. A man had stopped him at the Fennick gate. Not Harl. Not anyone from the gang. Jory said he talked like he came from over the bridge and he wasn't a dock man, his hands were too soft. He wanted a strong back for one night's loading off a lighter, and he'd pay three times the day rate. Half in hand." She lifts her chin toward the window. "It was a gold piece. Jory never held a gold piece in his life. He put it on this table and laughed at it."

Then she looks at the candle.

"I took that gold up the hill to the Lady's Hall the next morning, because I thought luck money should go back to the Lady. There's a side door where they sell candles to folk who won't be let in at the front. A young sister sold me that one. She said burn it till he's home." For the first time the steady voice slips, very slightly, and she puts it right. "He went out the next night. It was warm. Warm wind off the land, in this season, and him in his shirt-sleeves. He said he'd be back by the dawn bell with the other half."

She is quiet a moment. The candle in the saucer gutters and catches again.

"That's all I know." She looks straight at him across the white table. "Now you. Where have they put him?"

turns.message:
I sit on the stool she pointed at, and I put the hat on my knee, and I don't look at the jacket on the peg either.

"Straight, then. The mate — Teague — had the middle watch the night before they took your son out of the water. He says it was warm off the land, no weather behind it, and that one ship cleared the mole on it after second bell with no lamps: House Ammerhal's *Kindly Wind*. He won't say more than that, and I won't put words in his mouth. The Fist pulled a dockhand from the water off the Wide the next day. The dead-cart lads bring them up to the Seatower in the morning. That's where he'll be — or where he was. The porters say the drowned come out with a copper in their teeth, and the Fist says drink and writes nothing down."

I let her have that, and I keep my voice low. "I don't know why they've kept his name from you. I can think of reasons and none of them are kind. But I was a sergeant once, and the Fist still looks at a cloak like this before it looks at the face wearing it. I'll go out to the Seatower this afternoon and ask for him by name, as a man who served, and I'll make them write it in a book. If you want to come, you come with me. If you'd rather not stand in that tower a fifth time, I'll bring you back whatever they say, word for word."

Then, because I need it: "The soft-handed man from over the bridge. Did Jory say anything else about him — how he dressed, what he smelled of, which lighter, which quay? Anything a man would notice and a mother would remember him saying."
turns.reply:
James sits on the stool. The hat goes on his knee, and he keeps his eyes off the peg by the door.

Maud listens the way she listened on the step: hands folded on the white table, eyes on his face. At *Kindly Wind* she doesn't react. At *a copper in their teeth* her thumb presses once into the back of her other hand, hard, and lets go. When he says *write it in a book*, she breathes out through her nose. It isn't a laugh, though it comes close to one.

"A book." She looks at the candle in the window, then back at him. "Four times I went, and nobody wrote anything. A sergeant with a cloak, though. They'd write for that."

She gets up without being asked. She puts the pot back over the fire because her hands want something to do, and she answers his question with her back to him.

"He told it at this table like a joke. That's how I remember it." She moves the pot an inch, then back again. "The man called him *lad* the whole time, like a gentleman would. Jory said he had a dock coat on, but new, with no tar on it anywhere and stiff at the elbows. And he smelled like a barber's. Lavender water, Jory said, and he made a face, so I knew he meant a lot of it." She turns round. "The lighter wasn't coming to the Fennick. It was coming to the Fishgut Stair, below where the big ships lie. After second bell, when the tide turned. Jory said nobody unloads at the Fishgut at that hour. Then he laughed and said for triple, who cares."

She stops. The steady voice stays steady, but it takes her longer to find the next part.

"He asked could Jory swim." Her hand finds the edge of the table. "Jory told him no. Rope-walk lads never learn, there's no call to. And the man said good. Said that was safer. Nobody goes over the side showing off." She looks straight at James. "Jory thought that was funny. I thought it was a strange thing to want in a man you're hiring to carry crates."

The fire catches under the pot. Copper hasn't moved from the threshold. He has stopped watching the candle and is watching Maud.

"I'll come." She says it as if it was settled a while ago. "But not this afternoon. Peg Arlow's man went into the water two winters back. She was sick and couldn't go out to the tower, and when she could, they told her the unclaimed go out on the cart on the tenth day, to the pit past Rivington, under lime. No stone. No name." She takes the man's jacket off the peg at last, holds it for a moment, and puts it back. She takes her own shawl from the next peg down. "I don't know when they found him. Nobody told me that either. It's nine days since he went out."

She stands at her own door with the shawl in her tarred hands.

"So I'm asking you, Sergeant. Will you take me now?"

turns.message:
I'm on my feet before she's finished the question, hat back on my head.

"Yes. Now." I nod at the shawl. "Bring anything that says you're his mother — a pay chit, a letter, his name on paper from the Fennick gang if you've got one. Soldiers in tabards like paper. And leave the candle burning. The sister said till he's home."

At the door I stop and let Copper go out first, then hold it for her. "Walk beside me, not behind. I'll do the talking at the gate, and they'll look at the cloak before they look at either of us. When they ask, you say his name, clear, once. Then you let me be unpleasant about the book."

Down Rope Street I keep my pace to hers and keep an eye on the shed door at the bottom that swung shut behind the whittling boy. Then left along the quay, the water on our left this time, toward the Seatower.
turns.reply:
James is on his feet before she finishes asking, and the hat goes back on his head. Maud looks at him for a moment as if she hadn't expected the answer to come so fast. Then she nods once and goes to the dresser by the hearth.

She doesn't take long. She comes back with two things and holds them out flat on her tarred palm so he can see them. One is a wooden pay tally the length of a finger, notched along one edge and burned at the end with a brand of a crude F inside a ring. The other is a folded square of paper, greasy at the corners. It's a wage chit, a tenday's pay in a slanting foreman's hand: *J. Nettle, 6 days, Fennick. H.*

"Harl's hand," she says. "He writes them for the ones who can't count it themselves. Jory could, but he kept them anyway." The tally and the chit go into the pocket of her apron, under the shawl. She glances at the candle in the window and leaves it burning.

At the door James stops and lets Copper go out first. The cat steps down onto the scrubbed step, looks both ways along the street like a man crossing a road, and waits. Maud comes out under James's arm, pulls the door shut behind her and turns the key. Then she stands for a moment with her hand flat on the wood.

"Beside," she says. "Not behind. I heard you." She puts her chin up. "His name, clear, once. I can do that."

They go down Rope Street together under the washing. She walks quickly for a small woman, and James doesn't have to slow much. Two doors down a curtain moves. At the pump, a woman filling a bucket stops pumping and watches them pass. She says nothing, but she touches two fingers to her own lips and then to her heart as Maud goes by. Maud gives her a short nod back.

James keeps his eyes on the bottom of the street. The step where the whittling boy sat is still empty. The shed door that swung shut behind him is open now.

A man is leaning in that doorway, in no hurry at all. He's lean and somewhere past forty, clean-shaven, in a good brown coat buttoned to the throat. The coat isn't new and isn't tarred, and it's the plain kind a clerk wears when he doesn't want to look like one. James can see no weapon on him, which only means he isn't showing one. The whittling boy sits on an upturned bucket just inside the shed behind him, still working at the same peg.

The man straightens off the doorframe as they come down the last stretch of slope. He doesn't step into their path, but he stands where they have to pass him.

He takes his hat off. He does it to Maud first.

"Mistress Nettle." His voice is quiet, a Lower City voice with the corners sanded off. "I was sorry to hear Jory hadn't come home. We all were."

Maud stops. Her hand goes into her apron pocket and closes on the tally. Her voice doesn't change at all.

"His bit went to you every tenday. Harl paid it Fifthday mornings, regular." She looks at him the way she looked at James through a hand's width of door. "You were sorry nine days ago too, then. Nobody came to say so."

The man takes that without blinking, the way someone takes a debt he knows is owed. He doesn't argue. He turns to James and puts his hat back on.

"Ser. Nobody's stopping you." He says it plainly, as a fact. "This is our street, though, and our men are the ones going in the water. So when a Tethyrian in a regimental cloak walks up it on his second morning in the city, asks for Jory Nettle's house by name, and walks out with Jory Nettle's mother in her good shawl, the people I answer to will want to know why." He keeps his hands where James can see them, loose at his sides. "I'd rather ask you than guess. What's your business with the Nettles, and where are you taking her?"

Copper has sat down on the cobbles exactly between James's boots and the man's. He's looking at the boy's peg, not at the man.
